title: The Lemonade Detectives

subtitle.text: "Hey, Henry! Come out here!"
Henry looked out the window and saw his cousin waving at him from the sidewalk in front of his house.
Maggie was nine years old and lived next door.
Her mom and Henry's mom were sisters.
"What do you want?" Henry called down to Maggie. "I'm busy."
He glanced at his computer.
He'd just finished lunch, and now he was playing his favorite game, Puzzle Pirates.
All he had to do was solve one more puzzle, and he would reach Level Ten.
"Just come down here!" Maggie yelled again.
Henry sighed. He was two years older than Maggie, but that didn't stop her from bossing him around.
His best friend, Cole, always told him that he should just ignore her.
But Maggie was usually so loud and dramatic, she was hard to ignore!
Henry turned off his computer and headed outside.
Maggie was waiting for him and holding a handmade cardboard sign.
"Look at this," she said. "Isn't it awesome?"
The sign read: MAGGIE'S LEMONADE STAND
ONE CUP: 25 cents
TWO CUPS: 45 cents
BELLTOWN'S BEST BEVERAGE!
Maggie was very artistic. She'd drawn a glass of lemonade below the words.
It looked so realistic that it made Henry thirsty.
"Great sign," Henry said. "Maybe I'll buy a cup."
"You won't have to," Maggie said. "You'll get your lemonade for free."
Henry was instantly suspicious.
If Maggie was running a lemonade stand to make money, why would she give away the lemonade for free?
"What do you mean?" he asked.
She grinned. "You'll get it for free because you're an employee," she said.
"I hereby hire you to help me with my lemonade stand."
Henry rolled his eyes. "Are you kidding me?" he said.
"Lemonade stands are for babies."
Maggie scowled. "No, they're not!"
"Yes, they are," Henry said.
"Why do you want to do something like that anyway?"
"Mom and Dad said I can take horseback-riding lessons if I pay half of the cost myself," Maggie explained.
"I figured I could make lots of money selling lemonade while it's hot out.
I'll switch to hot chocolate when the weather turns cold."
"Sounds like a good plan," Henry said.
"So you'll help?" Maggie looked excited.
"Nope," Henry said.
Maggie tried to change his mind.
She promised him all the free lemonade he could drink.
Then she told him he could have 10 percent of the profits.
Henry just shook his head. "No, thanks," he said.
"Good luck with your new business. I'm going to Cole's."
He walked over to Cole's house on the next block.
The two of them played soccer for a while in Cole's yard.
Then they headed back to Henry's house to play Puzzle Pirates.
On the way they passed Maggie's lemonade stand.
The stand was a table set up on the sidewalk in front of Maggie's house.
Two teenage girls were standing nearby sipping lemonade from paper cups.
A boy with a skateboard was chugging his lemonade.
A little boy clung to his mother's hand while she leaned against the table and talked on her cell phone.
Maggie was nearby chatting with a kid named Nathan and his little sister, Nora.
It looked as if Nathan and Nora had just returned from the local swimming pool.
Their bathing suits were still wet.
When Maggie spotted Henry and Cole coming, she hurried to meet them.
"Want some lemonade?" she asked. "It's a dollar per cup."
"A dollar?" Henry said. "I thought you were charging 25 cents."
"Yeah!" Cole pointed to the sign. "It's written right there. See?"
Maggie tossed her head. "That's the price for normal people.
Rotten cousins and their friends get charged extra."
"Fine. I wasn't thirsty anyway," Henry said, rolling his eyes.
"Come on, Cole. We have plenty of soda at my house."
They started to walk away. But Maggie ran after them.
"Stop. I was just kidding," she said.
"I'll sell you lemonade for fifty cents per cup."
When the boys kept walking, she tried again. "Okay, okay! Twenty cents.
That's my special price for cousins and friends of cousins."
"You have a deal," Cole said, turning around.
Henry and Cole headed back to the lemonade stand.
Maggie poured them each a cup of lemonade.
Henry fished some change out of his pocket to pay for it.
Cole took a sip. "Hey, this lemonade is really good!"
Maggie smiled. "It's the best in town," she bragged.
"Everyone says so. I've made a ton of money already!"
She opened the cashbox on her table to put the boys' money away.
When she looked inside the box, she gasped.
"Oh no!" she cried. "My money is gone!"
"Who stole my money?" Maggie yelled loudly.
"Maggie," Henry warned, "you have to have proof before you start accusing people of stealing."
He looked into the cashbox that Maggie was holding.
It was completely empty.
"Are you sure you didn't take the money out and put it in your pocket or something?" he asked her.
"Yeah," Cole said. "You probably put the money somewhere."
"No way!" Maggie looked really upset now.
"There was a lot of cash in here five minutes ago when Mrs. Martin paid for little Marty's lemonade."
She pointed to the woman standing nearby, who was still talking on her cell phone.
The little boy, Marty Martin, had dropped his mother's hand.
He was staring at Maggie and banging a toy suitcase against his knees.
"Okay," Henry said.
"Then maybe the money blew away when you opened the box."
"It's not even windy today," Maggie said. She shook her head.
"I think someone stole my horseback-riding money.
And I want to know who it was!"
By now everyone except Mrs. Martin was staring at her.
The two teenage girls giggled and whispered to each other.
Maggie looked at them.
"Was it you two?" she asked. "Did you take my money?"
"No," one of the girls said. "We're not crooks.
Come on, Jill, let's get out of here."
"Yeah." Her friend giggled. "Before she accuses us of something else!"
The two of them laughed and walked off.
Maggie glared at them, and then looked around again.
"Maybe it was Ryan!" she said. Ryan had finished chugging his lemonade.
Now he was jumping his skateboard on and off the curb.
"Did you steal my money when I wasn't looking?" Maggie asked.
He stopped and stared at Maggie. "Dude, I didn't take your money.
Maybe you should have watched it better," he said.
Then he skated off down the street.
"Hey! Get back here!" Maggie yelled.
But Ryan ignored her, skidding around the corner.
Nathan and his little sister Nora were listening to everything.
"It wasn't me," Nathan said before Maggie could say anything to him. "I promise."
"Are you sure?" Maggie said. "It had to be someone!"
Nora poked her brother. "I think I hear Mommy calling us," she said.
"I didn't hear anything," Henry said.
"Me neither. But I'd better go check," Nathan said.
"Come on, Nora, let's go home."
"No!" Nora said. She loved to argue. "I don't want to!"
Nathan was used to her, so he just ignored her.
But when he rushed off toward their house, she hurried after him.
Maggie was looking around for more possible thieves.
"Where did Mrs. Martin and Marty go?" she asked.
"They left." Cole pointed down the block.
Henry looked and saw Mrs. Martin wandering away.
Her cell phone was still pressed to her ear.
Little Marty was skipping along after her.
"I don't think you need to accuse Mrs. Martin of being the thief," Henry said.
"She's a police detective, remember?"
Cole nodded. "She catches thieves—she's not one herself," he said.
"Maybe you're right." Maggie frowned.
"But someone stole my money, and I want to know who it was."
"Calm down," Henry told his cousin.
"You're not going to figure it out by yelling at everyone."
"How else am I going to get an answer?" Maggie asked.
"Think about it logically," Henry said.
"Whoever took that money is a thief, which means he or she is probably a liar too."
"Good point," Cole said with a nod.
"Guess you'd better say good-bye to that money, Maggie."
Maggie scowled at him. "Be quiet, Cole!"
"She doesn't need to give up," Henry told his friend.
"We just need to think like detectives.
I bet if the three of us work together, we can figure out who took the money."
"We're just kids," Maggie said.
"How are we supposed to think like detectives?"
"I know!" Cole said. "I watched a mystery movie on TV last week.
The detective started by figuring out who the suspects were."
"We already know that," Maggie interrupted.
"It had to be someone who was nearby when the money disappeared."
Henry smiled. "See? We're already thinking like detectives," he said.
"Okay, so we know approximately when the money disappeared.
Who was nearby during that time?"
"You just saw them," Maggie said.
"Nathan and Nora, Mrs. Martin and Marty, Ryan, and those two teenage girls.
Oh, and you two of course."
"Nobody else stopped by before Henry and I got here?" Cole asked.
"Like a stranger or a suspicious-looking deliveryman?"
Maggie shook her head. "Nope. Just the people you saw."
Cole bit his lip. "That means the thief had to be someone we know."
They all looked at each other.
"It's someone from our very own neighborhood!" said Henry.
"It's weird to think that someone from our neighborhood is a thief," Cole said.
"I know," Henry agreed.
"But Maggie's money is gone, which means that someone stole it.
All we have to do now is figure out who it was."
"Who are the suspects again?" Cole asked.
Maggie sighed. "Weren't you listening?" she said.
"There were only a few people close enough to the lemonade stand to grab the money.
They were Nathan and Nora, Mrs. Martin and Marty, Ryan, and those two teenage girls."
"I doubt it was Nathan," Cole said. "He's a nice kid."
Henry nodded. Nathan was the same age as him and Cole, and everyone liked him.
Kids liked him because he was always smiling and loved to have fun.
"That little sister of his is kind of weird though," Maggie pointed out.
"She's always making up crazy stories and dressing up in funny costumes and stuff."
"Nora is a bit strange," Henry agreed.
"But being weird isn't the same as being a thief.
Plus she's only five years old.
That's pretty young to steal money from a cashbox."
"What about Ryan, that kid who skateboards all the time?" Maggie said.
"He's always getting in trouble at school."
Ryan was three years younger than Henry.
Henry had seen him around, but he didn't know Ryan very well.
"What kind of trouble?" Henry asked Maggie.
She shrugged. "Mostly teachers get mad at him for goofing off and not paying attention in class."
"I heard he skateboarded into his neighbor's flowers," Cole said.
"He got in big trouble for that!"
"That doesn't make him a thief," Henry said.
"But he seems like a better suspect than the others.
Let's go find him and talk to him."
Maggie put a cover on her pitcher of lemonade so bugs wouldn't get in it.
Then the three kids headed down the block in the direction that Ryan had gone.
"What are we going to say when we find him?" Cole asked.
"I know what I want to say." Maggie frowned.
"I want to tell him to give me back my money!
Otherwise I'll break his skateboard in half!"
"I don't think that's a good idea, Maggie," Henry told her.
"We're not going to threaten Ryan.
We're just going to ask him a few questions, like my dad does when he's interviewing someone."
Henry's father was a journalist who wrote stories for the local newspaper.
He liked to say that his job was one part writing, one part asking questions, and three parts listening.
That was because he spent so much time interviewing people and listening to their answers.
"Wait. We're going to ask Ryan a few questions?" Cole said.
"I can only think of one question: Did you take the money?"
"Yeah," Maggie said. "And I already asked him that."
Henry had just spotted Ryan up ahead.
The skateboarder was practicing kick flips.
His baggy shorts fluttered when he jumped, and his sneakers squeaked when he landed.
"Just listen and play along," Henry whispered to Cole and Maggie.
"I'm going to interview Ryan, just like Dad would.
We might learn something by listening to his answers."
The other two looked skeptical. But Henry hurried forward.
"Hi, Ryan," he called out. "Can I talk to you for a second?"
Ryan finished his flip, and then rolled over to Henry on his skateboard.
"Sure, dude. What do you want to talk about?"
He grinned, shoving both hands in his pockets.
Henry smiled back.
"We're just trying to find out what happened to Maggie's money.
Since you were there, we thought you might have seen who took it."
"Nope. Sorry." Ryan shrugged.
"Okay," Henry said.
"Then did you see anyone hanging around the lemonade stand?
Maybe a stranger or something?"
"I already told you there was nobody else around, Henry," Maggie interrupted.
Then she glared at Ryan. "I know you stole my money.
Why don't you just admit it?"
"No way." Ryan glared back at her.
"Why should I admit to something I didn't do? I didn't take your money!"
"Well, somebody did," Cole pointed out.
"It was probably her." Ryan laughed and pointed at Maggie.
"What?" Maggie screeched. "Don't be ridiculous!
Why would I steal my own money?"
Ryan shrugged again. "How should I know?"
Henry looked away, thinking.
He still believed that Ryan was the most likely suspect, but this interview wasn't going well so far.
Henry tried to think of another question.
What would his dad ask? He couldn't think of anything.
Besides he was pretty sure that Ryan wouldn't answer any more questions.
Not after Maggie had just accused him of the crime again.
So how could they figure out if Ryan had done it?
"Are you guys ready to stop accusing me of stealing your money?" Ryan asked.
"Because I'm not going to stand here all day. See you later."
Without waiting for an answer, he skated off.
He stopped about half a block away and went back to practicing skateboarding tricks on the sidewalk.
"Well, that was a waste of time," Cole said.
Maggie watched Ryan do a fancy flip. "I still think he did it," she muttered.
Henry was thinking hard.
"If Ryan took that money, there must be a way to prove it."
"I know." Cole cracked his knuckles. "Ryan's a lot smaller than us.
We could hold him down and Maggie could search him."
"Great idea!" Maggie's eyes lit up. "Let's go get him!"
"Hold on." Henry grabbed Maggie's arm before she could rush down the block.
"We can't do that."
"Why not?" Maggie said. "He took my money!"
For a second it looked as if she were about to cry.
"I need that money for horseback-riding lessons."
"We don't know for sure that he's the thief," Henry reminded her.
"And it's not fair to gang up on him.
If he didn't take your money, we'll get in big trouble."
Maggie sighed. "I'm starting to think this investigation isn't worth it.
Maybe I should just go back to the lemonade stand and start over."
Cole nodded. "And maybe you should put a lock on your cashbox," he suggested.
"Good idea," Maggie said.
Henry couldn't believe his ears.
"You mean you guys are ready to give up already?
But we're only on our first suspect!"
Maggie shrugged. "Like you said, the thief is never going to admit to it.
So what's the point?"
"There has to be a way to figure out what happened."
Henry turned to look at Ryan.
Ryan was still ignoring them and practicing his skateboard tricks.
He did a couple of flips, and then jumped the skateboard off the sidewalk.
Henry stared at the shorts.
He could see the pockets open every time Ryan moved.
"If Ryan did take the money, he must have stuck it in his pockets," he murmured.
"There's nowhere else he could be holding it.
And he probably didn't have time to hide it anywhere between then and now."
"Good point." Cole nodded.
"Does that mean you want to hold him down and search him after all?"
"No. I have a better idea."
Henry hurried off toward Ryan before Maggie and Cole could respond.
Ryan stopped skating when he saw him coming.
"Oh, it's you again," he said, not sounding very happy.
"Don't worry. I'm not here to ask you any more questions."
Henry smiled at the younger kid.
"Actually I was just watching you skate. You've got some nice moves."
"Thanks, dude." Ryan looked suspicious but a little proud too.
"So can you do some of the harder tricks?" Henry asked.
"I saw a kid from Oakview School do some awesome tricks last weekend."
Maggie and Cole had caught up to him by now.
"Who cares what tricks he can do?" Maggie muttered.
"I can do tons of cool stuff," Ryan bragged.
"Way more than anybody from Oakview."
"I saw that kid do a handstand on his skateboard," Henry said.
"Can you do that?"
"Sure. Watch me." Ryan skated a short distance away from them.
Then he turned around and headed back toward them, kicking off with one foot to build up speed.
"Who cares if he can do a handstand?" Maggie said.
"Shh." Henry hushed her. "Just watch."
As he got closer, Ryan leaned down and grabbed the edges of the board with his hands.
A second later, he was upside-down with his legs in the air.
"Awesome!" Cole cheered, clapping. "You're really good."
"Thanks." Ryan flipped back onto his feet and stood up.
His face was red, and his pockets were turned inside out.
"I think you lost the stuff that was in your pockets," Henry said.
"I'll help you pick it up."
Henry stepped forward.
A little pile of stuff lay in the spot where Ryan had flipped himself upside down.
There was a peppermint candy, a house key, and a couple of snail shells.
Henry grabbed it all and handed it back to Ryan.
Then he said good-bye and hurried off around the corner.
His friends followed. "What was that all about?" Cole asked.
"Don't you get it?" Henry smiled. "I just proved that Ryan isn't our thief.
If he'd stolen Maggie's money, it would have fallen out of his pockets along with all that other stuff."
Cole's eyes widened. "Whoa! You're right!"
Maggie looked impressed too. But she didn't look happy.
"So now what?" she said. "If Ryan didn't take my money, then who did?"
Henry, Maggie, and Cole stood on the sidewalk staring at one another.
They'd just proven that Ryan hadn't stolen Maggie's cash.
But they weren't any closer to solving the mystery.
"I guess we should check out some of our other suspects," Henry said to Maggie and Cole.
"What about those two teenage girls?" Cole suggested.
"They left the scene of the crime pretty fast."
Maggie nodded. "True.
Plus they were whispering together the whole time they were at the lemonade stand, like they were planning something."
"Do you think they could have taken the money when you weren't looking?" Henry asked her.
"Sure," Maggie said.
"I had my back to the cashbox while I was talking to Nathan.
Anyone could have grabbed the money then."
"Okay, let's see if we can track down those girls," Henry said.
They walked back to the lemonade stand.
There was no sign of the two teenagers.
"I think they walked away in this direction," Cole said.
He pointed down the street.
The three of them walked to the end of the block, and then stopped.
"Which way should we go now?" Maggie wondered.
Henry looked around and spotted Mrs. Smith watering flowers on her front porch.
She smiled and waved when she saw them.
"Hot day, isn't it?" she called.
"It sure is," Henry replied politely.
"Mrs. Smith, did you happen to see two teenage girls walk past here recently?"
"Do you mean Jill and Ashley?" Mrs. Smith nodded.
"Yes, they passed by about ten or fifteen minutes ago.
They were heading toward town."
"Thanks," Henry said. Then he looked at his friends. "Come on. Let's go."
They walked another few blocks until they reached Main Street.
Lots of people were going in and out of the shops and restaurants.
"How are we supposed to find those two girls now?" Cole asked, looking around.
"They could be anywhere."
"Not really," Henry said.
"I doubt they're in the dry cleaner's or the hardware store.
Teenage girls don't usually go to stores like that."
"True." Maggie was looking around too.
"And it's the middle of the afternoon, so they're probably not at any of the restaurants."
"I bet they're in the drugstore or the bakery," Cole said.
"Maybe we should check the bakery first," he added, licking his lips.
Henry grinned.
He knew that Cole loved the bakery's doughnuts more than almost any other food.
But Henry didn't want to waste any time.
"The drugstore is closer," he pointed out.
"Let's go there first, and then we'll look in the bakery.
If they're not in either place, we could start checking some of the other stores."
The three friends headed across the street to Herman's Drugstore.
As soon as he stepped inside, Henry heard loud giggles.
"Listen! That sounds like them," he whispered to his friends.
He followed the giggling sounds to the makeup aisle.
Jill and Ashley were halfway down the aisle, looking at a display of brightly colored nail polish and lip gloss.
They didn't notice Henry watching them because they were too busy grabbing stuff from the shelves.
"This is nice," Jill exclaimed, tossing a bottle of sparkly nail polish in a shopping basket.
"It's kind of expensive, isn't it?" Ashley said. Then she giggled.
"Oops, never mind. Who cares if it's expensive? We have plenty of money!"
"Yeah." Jill giggled and reached for some lip gloss.
"I think I'll buy this too."
Ashley grabbed two more tubes of lip gloss.
"We might as well get a few extras. After all we can afford it!"
"True," her friend agreed with another loud giggle.
"After we finish here, let's go pick out some candy."
"And then I want to look at the magazines," Ashley said.
Henry's eyes widened.
The teenagers were acting as if they had lots of money to spend!
"I knew it! Those two did it!" Maggie said from behind him.
"They stole my money!"
Her voice was kind of loud. The two older girls heard her and looked over.
"Hey, it's that girl with the lemonade stand," Jill said.
"Shouldn't you be home squeezing lemons or something?"
Ashley started giggling all over again.
Maggie marched over and pointed into their shopping basket.
"Where'd you get the money to buy all that stuff?" she demanded.
Ashley shot a look at Jill.
Jill frowned and looked down at the floor.
For a second neither of them answered.
Henry traded looks with Cole.
"Is it my imagination," he whispered, "or are those two acting awfully suspicious?"
It wasn't Henry's imagination.
The two teenage girls were definitely acting suspicious.
They grabbed their shopping basket and rushed away, disappearing around the end of the aisle.
"Hey, wait!" Henry called after them.
"Come back here! We want to talk to you."
He rushed after the girls, with Maggie and Cole right behind him.
"They did it!" Maggie exclaimed.
"They stole my money! I should have known it was them!"
"Just hold on," Henry told her over his shoulder.
"Don't start accusing them of stealing your money until I get a chance to ask them some questions."
They caught up to Jill and Ashley near the back of the store.
The two girls seemed annoyed when they saw the younger kids coming again.
"Why are you following us around?" Ashley demanded.
"We just wanted to say hi," said Henry.
"Maggie likes to keep in touch with her best customers. Right, Maggie?"
"Right," Maggie said, glaring at the older girls.
Henry was afraid she was going to say something rude to them.
But she kept quiet.
"So you guys are doing a lot of shopping today, huh?"
Henry said, glancing into the girls' shopping basket.
"Not really." Jill shot a look at Ashley. "We were just kidding around."
"That's right," Ashley agreed quickly.
"We're not really buying all this stuff. See? We're putting it back."
She reached into the basket, grabbed lip gloss, and stuck it back on the shelf.
Jill did the same thing with a pack of gum.
"That's weird," Cole said.
"Why would you pick up all that stuff if you weren't planning to buy it?"
Ashley shrugged. "I told you. We were just goofing around, having fun."
"That doesn't seem like much fun to me," Cole commented.
"Well, playing basketball doesn't seem like fun to me," Ashley snapped.
"And boys do that all the time, right?"
Cole was surprised. "What do you mean? Basketball is a blast!"
Henry glanced over at Maggie.
She was getting that impatient look on her face again.
"You two aren't fooling me," she burst out.
"I know what you were doing. You were getting ready to spend my money!"
"What are you talking about?" Jill asked.
"You know what I'm talking about!" Maggie went on.
"Someone stole the money from my lemonade stand!"
Ashley laughed. "Oh, right. I forgot about that."
"You mean you never found that money?" Jill added.
"Did you ask Ryan, that kid who's always skateboarding?
He's a troublemaker. He crashed into my mom's flowers a couple of weeks ago."
"It wasn't Ryan. It was you two!" Maggie insisted.
"No, it wasn't," Ashley said. "Why would we need a few dollars? We already have—"
"Quiet!" Jill hissed, elbowing her friend in the ribs.
"Oops." Ashley had a guilty expression on her face.
Then she shrugged. "But what's the big deal?" she asked Jill.
"We already agreed we're not going to use it."
"Use what?" Henry asked, feeling confused.
What were the girls talking about?
Jill had a guilty expression too.
She reached into the shopping basket and grabbed a candy bar.
She stuck it on a nearby shelf.
"It's nothing," she said.
"Maybe you'd better tell us," Cole suggested.
"Because you two are acting pretty suspicious."
"It's no big deal," Ashley said.
"Jill's mother gave us a fifty-dollar bill.
We were supposed to use it to buy sunscreen and some other stuff we need for summer camp."
Jill nodded. "We thought my mom wouldn't notice if we bought a few extra things.
But I guess we got carried away."
"Yeah. We realized it when you guys started asking us all those annoying questions."
Ashley shrugged. "So thanks, I guess."
Henry smiled. "You're welcome," he said.
Maggie was staring at them. "You mean you really didn't take my money?"
"Nope," Jill said.
"Besides we could buy a lot more with my mom's fifty dollars than we could with your two or three dollars."
"It was much more than that," Maggie corrected her.
"That's why I want to get it back!
I need it so I can take horseback-riding lessons."
"Oh. Good luck," Ashley said. She sounded more sympathetic now.
Jill seemed thoughtful. "I just remembered something," she said.
"I saw that little girl Nora grabbing something off the table while you were busy talking to her brother.
I thought she was just getting a napkin or something, but she was pretty close to that cashbox.
And she was acting kind of sneaky."
"Really?" Maggie said.
Henry and Cole looked at each other.
"I guess we know who to investigate next," said Henry.
"Do you really think Nora took the money?" Cole asked.
"I don't know," Henry said. "She's just a little kid.
And she has always seemed pretty honest to me. Remember?
She even told the bus driver that his hairpiece looked fake."
Cole laughed. "I almost forgot about that," he said.
"Good thing the bus driver has a sense of humor!"
Maggie was several steps ahead of them.
She was in such a hurry to reach Nathan and Nora's house that she was almost jogging.
"Hurry up!" she called over her shoulder.
"I want to get my money back and open up my lemonade stand again."
Henry walked a little faster until he caught up with Maggie.
"I wonder why Nora would steal your money," he said.
"She seems pretty young to do something like that."
"That's true." Cole had caught up by then too.
"It's hard to believe that Nora suddenly decided to rob Maggie's lemonade stand all by herself."
He looked worried. "I just thought of something.
What if Nora and Nathan were in cahoots?"
"In cahoots?" Maggie echoed. "What the heck does that mean?"
"I heard it on that detective movie I saw on TV," Cole said.
"When someone's in cahoots, it means they're working together."
Henry nodded. "I see what you mean.
If Nathan and Nora were in cahoots, then Nathan could have distracted Maggie on purpose by talking to her.
He kept her distracted long enough for Nora to grab the money out of the cashbox.
Then once they got away, the two of them could have split the cash between them."
Maggie's eyes widened. "Do you really think that's what happened?"
"No," Henry said. "I don't think Nathan is like that."
"Yeah, I don't either," Cole agreed. "Maybe it was just Nora after all.
We already know she's a weird kid.
Nathan says she acts sneaky and secretive all the time.
Maybe she's a thief too."
"Maybe." Henry still had a hard time believing Nora was the culprit.
Something was bugging him about the whole situation, though he couldn't figure out what it was.
Then again those teenage girls had seen Nora grab something off the table.
That definitely made the little girl seem guilty.
Besides they were almost out of suspects.
Soon they were turning the corner onto Nathan and Nora's street.
From halfway down the block, they spotted Nora talking and laughing with another girl.
"Looks like Nora has a friend over," Cole commented.
"I don't care," Maggie said. "I'm going to get my money back."
"Slow down." Henry grabbed her by the arm.
"You can't just march up to her and demand your money back."
"Oh yeah? Says who?" Maggie said.
"Think about it," Henry said. "We already know that Nora likes to argue.
If you accuse her of being the thief, she'll just argue, whether she did it or not."
"Well, what else can I do?" asked Maggie.
"She and her friend haven't seen us yet.
Let's hide and spy on them for a little while," Henry suggested.
"Yeah. Like a stakeout!" Cole grinned.
"The detectives in that mystery movie did that.
They sat in their car in front of a suspect's house all night!"
"I don't want to sit around here all night."
Maggie still sounded a little grumpy.
But she followed the boys as they tiptoed behind a hedge that ran along the side of the yard.
The three of them crouched down behind the hedge.

And her voice was always pretty loud.
A second later he heard the sound of running feet.
When he jumped out from behind the shrub, he saw Nora running away.
"She heard us," he called to his friends. "Come on, let's catch her!"
"Nora!" Nathan yelled as they all started running. "Stop!"
But Nora didn't stop. That was no surprise, at least to Henry.
As far as he could tell, Nora hardly ever did anything anyone told her to do!
Nora was a pretty fast runner for a little kid.
She raced across the yard and disappeared through the hedge.
"She's in the neighbors' yard," Maggie said. "Hurry!"
Henry ran as fast as he could toward the hedge.
It was too thick to see anything on the other side.
But he kept his eyes on the spot where Nora had pushed through.
Cole was the fastest of all of them, so he got there first.
"Ahh!" he yelled as he pushed through the hedge.
"Hey, where'd she go?" he called from the other side.
Henry pushed through the hedge too.
He looked around and saw Cole standing there.
A second later Maggie and Nathan appeared.
But there was no sign of Nora.
"Uh-oh," Cole said. "Do you think she's hiding?"
Nathan was out of breath after all the running, so it took him a second to answer.
"Probably," he said. "She likes to hide.
Once she hid in the basement and my parents couldn't find her for over an hour."
Henry looked around the neighbors' yard.
It was smaller than Nathan and Nora's yard, but there were plenty of places to hide.
There was a large vegetable garden with lots of big tomato plants, a patch of corn, and teepees covered with bean vines.
The rest of the yard had shrubs and flowers, a birdbath, and a sculpture of a dog.
At the back of the yard was the same forest that ran behind all the houses on the block.
"Let's spread out and search for her," Henry decided.
"Nathan, you go that way and search the neighbors' flower beds.
Maggie, check the front yard and the other side of the house.
Cole, make sure she's not hiding out in the woods.
I'll check the vegetable garden."
"Okay," Nathan said, and the others nodded. Then they split up.
Henry hurried over to the vegetable garden.
He peeked behind every tomato plant and bean teepee.
He looked into the corn patch. He even checked under the wheelbarrow.
But there was no sign of Nora.
By the time he finished searching, his friends were coming back.
"I didn't see her," Maggie reported.
"Me neither," Cole said. "What about you, Nathan?"
"Nope," Nathan said. "Did you find anything, Henry?"
Henry shook his head and sighed. "It looks like Nora got away from us."
Henry could hardly believe that Nora had outsmarted them.
She had led them into the neighbors' yard and then disappeared.
But he wasn't ready to give up yet.
"I have an idea," he told Maggie, Cole, and Nathan.
"Nora probably waited for us to start looking for her.
Then she sneaked back through the hedges.
If we hurry, we might be able to find her before she makes it to the house."
Nathan nodded. "Let's go," he said.
He led The Lemonade Detectives through the hedge into his own yard.
They got there just in time to see Nora racing toward the house.
"Stop right there!" Nathan yelled loudly. "We caught you, Nora!"
They ran toward her.
Just then the back door flew open and Nora's parents rushed out.
"Oh no!" Nora's mom exclaimed. "She got out again!"
Nora's dad looked worried. "Hush, don't wake her," he told his wife.
"Someone told me you're never supposed to wake a sleepwalker."
"She's not really sleepwalking, Dad!" Nathan said.
Henry had been watching Nora.
As soon as she'd seen her parents, she'd closed her eyes and held out both arms in front of her.
Henry thought she looked more like a zombie than a sleepwalker.
But her act seemed to be fooling her parents.
"That's not a nice thing to say, son," Nathan's father scolded.
"Your sister could get hurt if she keeps sleepwalking like this.
I wonder how she got outside this time."
"She climbed out her bedroom window," Nathan said.
"That's enough, Nathan," his father said. "This is no time for jokes."
"Come with me, sweetie," Nora's mother said softly as she started guiding Nora toward the house.
"Let's get you safely back to bed."
"It's time for you to come inside too," Nathan's father told Nathan.
Then he glanced at Henry, Maggie, and Cole.
"And you kids had better head home. It's getting late."
"Late? It's not even eight o'clock yet," Maggie said.
Henry grabbed his cousin by the arm and pulled her toward the front of the house.
"Yes, we'd better go," he told Nathan's dad politely.
"See you tomorrow, Nathan."
Now that Nora had been caught "sleepwalking" again, Henry guessed that her parents would watch her very closely.
She probably wouldn't be able to sneak out again that night.
That meant any more detective work would have to wait until the next day.
The following morning Henry was eating breakfast when Maggie hurried in through the kitchen door.
"Good morning, Maggie," said Henry's mother, who was also Maggie's aunt.
"Would you like some scrambled eggs?"
"No thanks, Aunt Susan. I already ate."
Maggie sat down at the table across from her cousin.
"Hurry up, Henry," she said.
"I want to go back to Nora and Nathan's house and investigate."
"Okay," Henry said. "Let's call Cole and tell him to meet us there."
Nathan was waiting in front of his house when the three detectives got there.
"What's the plan for today?" he asked.
"Do you have any theories about what Nora is doing when she sneaks out?"
"Not yet," Henry admitted. "But at least we know she's not sleepwalking."
Cole nodded. "She was wide-awake when she ran away from us, that's for sure."
"I still think she was heading for the tree house when she heard us," Maggie said.
"Maybe we should search for clues up there."
Nathan seemed doubtful. "Why would she sneak around just to go to my tree house?" he asked.
"She's allowed to climb up there whenever she wants, as long as she tells someone where she's going."
"Really?" Cole said. "My friend Bruce never lets his little sisters in his tree house."
"Nathan must be much nicer than your friend Bruce," Maggie said with a laugh.
"Anyway, I still think we should look in the tree house."
"You're right, Maggie," Henry agreed.
"It's worth checking out, just in case."
All four of them hurried past the house to the backyard.
Then they climbed up the ladder leading into Nathan's tree house.
"Wow," Cole said, looking around.
"This place is really cool, Nathan!
You can see half the neighborhood from up here."
Henry wasn't very interested in the view.
He was busy looking around for anything suspicious.
But all he saw were some empty candy wrappers and Nathan's favorite comic books.
There was no sign that Nora had been in the tree house recently.
"Oh well," Henry said. "I guess this idea isn't working.
Maybe we'll have to wait until tonight to try another stakeout."
"Okay," Maggie said, and Nathan nodded.
Cole wasn't listening. He was still looking out the window.
"Hey, check it out!" he said.
"Nora just climbed out the playroom window again and is sneaking across the yard!"
Henry rushed over to the tree house window.
Cole was right! Nora was tiptoeing across the backyard.
She stopped every few steps and stared around in every direction.
"Shh!" he warned the others. "Don't let her hear us up here!"
Nora didn't look up as she passed beneath the tree house.
She turned left and hurried toward the picket fence at the side of the yard.
"Where's she going?" Maggie whispered.
Nora reached the fence and stepped over it. Then she kept walking.
"It looks like she's cutting across the Smiths' yard," Nathan said. "Let's follow her!"
They all climbed down from the tree house as fast as they could.
Henry led the way as they hurried after Nora.
"Will your neighbors mind that we're in their yard?"
Cole asked Nathan as he hopped over the fence.
Nathan shook his head. "They're really nice.
They said we can play over here anytime we want."
Henry was glad to hear that. But he was more focused on keeping Nora in sight.
"She's heading for the woods," he whispered to his friends. "Let's go!"
They raced to the edge of the forest.
There was a trail just inside the tree line.
Henry and his friends followed the trail as quietly as they could.
"Do you see her?" Maggie asked quietly.
"Not yet. Let's stop and listen," Henry whispered.
They all stopped and listened for a few seconds.
There were a lot of sounds in the woods.
Birds chirped in the branches overhead.
A squirrel rustled against pine needles as it scampered up a pine tree.
Bees buzzed around looking for flowers.
Then Henry heard something else: the crack of a twig somewhere deeper in the forest!
"Did you hear that?" he whispered.
The others nodded.
Henry spotted a smaller trail that turned off the main one.
Following the new trail, he walked toward the spot where he'd heard the cracking sound.
His friends were right behind him.
Then they all heard another sound: Thump!
"What was that?" Maggie whispered.
Henry didn't answer. He was already running toward the sound.
It had to be Nora!
He burst out into a small clearing.
There was an old toolshed in the middle of it.
Its rickety door was open—that was what had caused the thumping sound.
Standing in the doorway, with her back to them, was Nora!
"She's here!" Henry cried.
"Eek!" Nora spun around and let out a squeak of fright.
"What are you doing here?"
"We were following you."
Henry walked toward her, glad that she wasn't running away this time.
"What are you doing out here?"
"None of your business," Nora said.
Maggie, Cole, and Nathan rushed into the clearing.
"There she is!" Maggie exclaimed.
"You guys should stop sneaking around like that!" Nora cried loudly.
"You scared me! I had no idea you were following me!"
Henry stared at her. "Why isn't she trying to run away?" he wondered.
Last night she'd seemed desperate to get away from them.
"What's going on?" he demanded.
"Are you really surprised to see us, or are you faking?"
"What are you talking about, Henry?" Maggie pushed past him.
"Let's see what's in that shed."
Henry was still watching Nora suspiciously.
But he was curious about the shed too. He followed the others inside.
"Aha!" Nathan pointed to something in the corner.
"That explains everything!"
It was dark inside the shed.
Henry had to lean forward to see what Nathan was pointing at.
"Soda cans?" he said when he got a good look. "I don't get it."
"Nora isn't allowed to drink soda," Nathan explained as he picked up a can.
"She must have been sneaking out here to drink it."
Cole laughed. "I'm not allowed to drink soda either.
But I never thought of sneaking into the woods to drink it!"
Henry opened the shed door wider.
That let in more light so it was easier to see.
He counted three more empty soda cans lying in the corner.
"Please don't tell Mom and Dad!" Nora begged Nathan.
"I'll be in big trouble!"
Nathan sighed. "All right. But only if you promise not to do it anymore."
Nora crossed her heart.
"I promise I won't sneak out here to drink soda anymore," she said.
Then she dashed out of the shed and disappeared into the woods.
"Case closed!" Cole grinned.
"It looks like The Lemonade Detectives solved another tough mystery!"
"That's right." Nathan pulled a five-dollar bill out of his pocket.
"Here's your payment. Thanks!"
"Wait." Henry stepped forward and stopped Maggie from taking the money.
"What's the matter this time?" Maggie said.
"Keep your money for now, Nathan," Henry said with a frown.
"Because I don't think we've really solved your case."
"What do you mean, Henry?" Cole looked confused. "We just solved the case!
Nora was sneaking out here to drink soda!"
"Nora confessed," Maggie agreed.
"We should be happy that she didn't argue for once."
"But that's just it."
The more Henry thought about it, the more certain he was that he was right.
"Since when does Nora give up so easily?"
"It does seem strange." Nathan frowned.
"But she does love soda. And we caught her in the act."
"Did we?" Henry looked at each of them.
"Or is Nora even sneakier than we thought?
Maybe she saw us go up in the tree house so she sneaked past on purpose."
"Why would she do that?" Maggie asked.
Henry shrugged. "To make us think we'd solved the case.
That way, once we stop paying attention to her, she can go back to doing whatever she's really doing."
"But Nathan said she's not allowed to drink soda," Maggie said.
"So it makes sense that she'd sneak around for something like that.
Remember how she sneaked an extra cup of lemonade from my stand?"
"Yes," Henry said. "But this still doesn't make sense to me.
Why would she hide the soda this far from her house?"
"So her parents wouldn't find it," Cole said. "That's obvious."
Henry shook his head. "There are tons of closer hiding places."
"I guess so." Maggie looked around. "But this shed is a pretty good spot.
She could sit inside and drink the soda, and nobody would ever see her."
Nathan frowned again. "Now that I think about it, she hates places like this shed."
He stepped inside. "It's dark in here, and there are a ton of spiders and other bugs.
Nora does not like bugs!"
"I forgot about that," Maggie said.
"When she bought lemonade from me, she double-checked to make sure there were no bugs in it." She shrugged.
"But so what? Maybe she decided soda was more important than bugs."
"Maybe," Henry said. They started walking through the woods, still talking about the case.
"But why would she sneak out after her bedtime just to drink soda?
She could do it just as easily during the day."
"I guess that's true," Nathan agreed, looking thoughtful.
Maggie still didn't look convinced.
"We already know that Nora is weird," she said.
"Nothing she does makes a lot of sense."
"It does seem strange that there are only four empty cans in the shed," said Cole.
"How many times has she sneaked out?"
"More than four times," Nathan said.
Henry could tell that his friends were starting to believe him.
"Also, when we saw her sneaking out yesterday, she wasn't heading toward the Smiths' yard," he said.
"Remember? She was walking straight past the tree house toward the back of her own yard."
"You're right!" Maggie's eyes widened.
"Do you really think she tricked us into following her here?"
"But why?" Cole looked more confused than ever. "What's she really doing?"
"That's what we still have to figure out before we accept Nathan's money," Henry said.
Maggie sighed loudly. "Maybe you're right," she told Henry.
"Mom says you're the most logical person she knows.
And Nora is definitely the sneakiest kid in the neighborhood.
We should make sure she's not tricking us."
"Yeah," Cole agreed. "But how?"
"Good question," Nathan said.
They all turned to look at Henry. He smiled.
"Nora is sneaky," he said. "That means we have to be sneakier than she is."
"Okay," Cole said. "But how?"
Henry thought for a second.
The bad news was that they still had no idea what Nora was really doing when she sneaked out.
Their investigation had failed so far.
But the good news was that Nora thought she'd tricked them.
She wouldn't expect them to keep investigating after they'd solved the case.
That meant she wouldn't be as careful next time she sneaked out.
"I have a plan," Henry told his friends. "It's time for another stakeout."
Maggie groaned. "Again?" she said.
"But my favorite horse show is on TV tonight!
I don't want to miss it, especially since it seems like I'll never earn enough money for riding lessons!"
"You'll have enough money before long, Maggie," Henry said, smiling.
"And you can record your show and watch it later.
It'll be worth missing it tonight."
Cole looked doubtful. "Are you sure?" he said.
"Even if Nora thinks we gave up, she'll still be sneaking around so her parents don't catch her.
How are we supposed to follow her without being seen?"
"Don't worry," Henry said. "I told you I have a plan.
This isn't going to be an ordinary stakeout."
"What do you mean?" Nathan asked.
Henry winked. "This time our stakeout is going to have an extra-special, detective twist!"
"Are you ready?" Henry asked Maggie.
It was later that day.
The Lemonade Detectives were hiding behind a car parked near Nora's house.
They were getting ready to put the first step of Henry's plan into action.
Maggie made a face.
"Why do I have to be the one to distract Nora?" she complained.
"You're the only one who can distract her well enough," Henry said.
"Yeah." Cole laughed. "Nora would never believe it if Henry and I suddenly wanted to play princesses with her!"
"I guess you're right," Maggie said.
"But being a detective is harder than I thought!"
"Good luck." Henry peeked out from behind the car.
"She just came outside. See if you can keep her in the front yard, okay?"
"Okay." Maggie stood up and waved at Nora.
"Hi, Nora! What are you doing?" she called in a super-friendly voice.
"Wow," Cole whispered. "She's a pretty good actress."
Henry grinned. "Mom always says Maggie is very dramatic. I guess she's right."
He looked out from behind the car again.
Nora was twirling on her tiptoes while Maggie watched.
"It looks like Nora is distracted," he told Cole.
"We should be able to sneak through the neighbors' yard so she won't see us."
Cole nodded. "Don't forget the flour."
Henry picked up the bag of flour sitting by his feet.
Nathan had borrowed it from his family's kitchen.
It was an important part of Henry's plan.
"I've got it," Henry said. "Let's go."
That evening Henry and Maggie met Cole at Nora's house again.
They all hid behind the hedge. It was time for step two of Henry's plan.
"Is Nathan coming?" Cole whispered.
Henry shook his head. "I told him to stay inside and act normal.
That might keep Nora from getting suspicious."
"Good idea," Maggie said.
"If he's home when she goes to bed, she'll never think we're still investigating her."
Henry nodded. "Let's get to the tree house."
Soon all three of them were in Nathan's tree house.
Cole went over to the window. "All we have to do now is wait," he said.
"We can take turns watching for Nora to come outside," Henry suggested.
"I'll go first," Cole said.
"You two probably won't even have to take turns.
Last time Nora sneaked out right after she went to bed."
Maggie nodded, looking hopeful.
"Maybe I'll get home in time to see my TV show after all," she said.
"It's not on until eight-thirty."
"I thought you were recording it," Cole said.
"I am," Maggie replied. "But I'd rather see it live."
They all settled down to wait.
Cole sat by the window watching the house while Henry and Maggie played cards.
Half an hour passed. Cole stretched. "I'm bored," he said.
"It's time for somebody else to take a turn."
"I'll do it," Henry offered.
He traded places with Cole. When he looked out, the yard was quiet.
From the tree house, it was easy to see the back door, the playroom window, and Nora's bedroom window.
Another half hour went by.
Henry's eyes were getting tired from staring at the house.
"Maybe Nora isn't going to sneak out tonight," he said.
Cole looked up from flipping through one of Nathan's comic books.
"Or maybe she was telling us the truth," he said.
"Maybe she really was sneaking out to drink soda in that shed."
Henry still didn't believe Nora's story about the soda.
It didn't seem logical. But Nora wasn't a very logical person.
Could Cole be right?
"It's probably after eight o'clock by now," said Maggie.
"I'll have to leave soon if I want to watch my show."
"Let's just wait another few minutes," Henry said.
"Maybe Nora is being extra careful.
Her parents are probably checking on her a lot."
He looked out again.
It was getting darker, and there were deep shadows in the woods.
But it was still easy to see Nora's house.
Finally Maggie stood up. "I'm going home.
There's no point in missing my show if Nora's not going to sneak out tonight."
Henry was disappointed.
He and Cole had spent a long time setting up their special detective trick.
They'd used the whole bag of flour!
"Maybe you're right and she's not going to sneak out tonight," he said with a sigh.
He glanced at the house one more time. Then he gasped.
"Wait!" he whispered. "Here she comes!"
"Really?" Maggie said.
She and Cole rushed to the window.
They all watched Nora climb out her bedroom window and hurry across the backyard.
"She's heading straight for the woods," Maggie whispered.
Cole nodded. "She's definitely not heading toward the soda shed!"
Henry smiled. His feeling had been right!
Now all they had to do was figure out what Nora was really doing.
"Let's go after Nora!" Maggie whispered.
She sounded excited now. "She's almost reached the woods!"
"No, let's wait for a few seconds," Henry said.
"We don't want her to hear us following her."
He watched Nora until she disappeared into the woods.
A few seconds later there was a glow from just inside the tree line.
"It looks like she brought a flashlight," Cole said.
Henry nodded. "That should make it a lot easier to spot her.
Come on, I think it's safe to climb down now. She's too far away to hear us."
He led the way down from the tree house.
The three detectives hurried across the yard toward the woods.
"It's getting kind of dark," Maggie said, peering at the trail that led into the forest.
"I hope we'll be able to see."
"Don't worry. I brought a flashlight too." Henry pulled it out.
He stepped onto the shadowy trail.
It was time to put step three of his plan into action.
Henry waited a second longer, and then turned on his flashlight.
He shined it around until he found the flour that he and Cole had sprinkled on the ground earlier that day.
"Wow," Maggie said. "You guys sure used a lot of flour."
Cole grinned. "We used the whole bag.
I hope Nathan's parents don't decide to bake a cake anytime soon."
"Using a lot of flour was the only way my plan would work," Henry explained to Maggie.
"We had to sprinkle enough on the ground so that Nora would be sure to step in it."
Cole nodded. "Now all we have to do is follow her footprints," he said.
"I always knew Henry was smart, but this has to be the coolest plan ever!"
"I hope Nora didn't see the flour and jump over it," Maggie said, worried.
"I thought about that," Henry said.
"That's why we made sure to put it here in the woods, under the trees, instead of out in the yard.
It gets dark here a lot sooner than it does out there."
"Good thinking!" Maggie was impressed.
"Nora didn't turn on her flashlight right away.
So she probably didn't see the flour."
Cole grinned. "That's what we were hoping she'd do."
Henry was shining his flashlight up and down the line of flour.
"There!" he cried, spotting some powdery, white footprints leading deeper into the woods.
They had to be Nora's!
He followed the footprints, keeping his flashlight aimed at the ground.
His friends crept along behind him.
"The footprints are getting fainter already," Maggie whispered.
"I guess it didn't take long for most of the flour to come off Nora's shoes.
What if the footprints run out before we catch up to her?"
"If that happens, at least we'll know what direction she's going," Henry whispered back.
"And it's definitely not toward that shed where she pretended she was going before," Cole added.
"It's a good thing that Henry was too smart to fall for that!"
"Are you saying I wasn't smart enough?" Maggie asked, sounding insulted.
"Shh!" Henry hushed them. "I don't want her to hear us coming!"
Maggie and Cole stayed quiet after that.
The three friends tiptoed through the woods, following the faint flour footprints.
It was getting so dark that the woods seemed a little spooky.
Insects and frogs chirped all around the kids, and an owl hooted in the distance.
But Henry stayed focused on the footprints.
They were getting fainter and fainter. Finally they disappeared completely.
"Uh-oh," Cole whispered. "It's the end of the trail!"
Henry turned off his flashlight and looked around.
It was hard to see anything in the darkness.
But then he saw something up ahead—a light!
"Look!" he whispered. "That must be Nora's flashlight."
"Let's go get her!" Maggie whispered eagerly.
The three of them hurried toward the light, moving as quietly as they could.
Henry was in the lead as they emerged into a clearing.
On the far side was a huge oak tree.
The light was coming from the base of the tree.
Nora was there, leaning over. Her back was to the detectives.
She hadn't heard or seen them yet.
Henry squinted, trying to see what she was doing, but he couldn't tell.
He was about to whisper to his friends that they should hide behind the trees and watch Nora.
But Maggie was already pushing past him.
"Freeze, Nora!" she said loudly. "We caught you!"
Nora spun around and gasped. "Oh no!" she cried in surprise.
Henry hurried toward Nora, who was huddled against the tree.
"What are you doing over there?" he asked.
"None of your business!" Nora cried, looking upset.
"Do you guys hear something?" Maggie asked.
A high-pitched sound was coming from the tree trunk.
At first Henry thought it was an insect or a frog. Then he heard it again.
"It sounds like—," he began.
"Kittens!" Maggie cried.
"Look, there's a mother cat and a bunch of adorable kittens!"
Nora burst into tears. "Please don't tell anyone!" She sobbed.
"If Mom and Dad find out, they'll take Patches and her babies to the shelter!
They said I couldn't have any pets!"
Henry glanced at his friends.
He remembered what Nathan had told them about Nora wanting a pet.
She must have found this cat and her kittens and decided to take care of them in secret.
"It's okay, Nora," Maggie said.
"We'll make sure nothing bad happens to Patches and her kittens. I promise."
"Really?" Nora wiped her eyes.
"Really." Maggie reached in and tickled a kitten under its chin.
"Aw, they're so cute!"
"Come on, Nora," Henry said. "We'd better get you home."
The next day Henry met Cole at the lemonade stand.
"Where's Maggie?" Cole asked. "I was hoping for some lemonade."
"She'll be here soon," Henry said.
"She offered to walk over to Nathan's house to pick up our five-dollar fee."
"Cool! I already know how I'm going to spend my share." Cole grinned.
"I want glow-in-the-dark laces for my soccer shoes."
"We definitely earned our fee this time," Henry said.
"That was a tricky case!
At least now we know why Nora sneaked out mostly at night.
She didn't want anyone to see her carrying cans of tuna into the woods."
Cole nodded. "I feel sorry for her.
She seemed really upset about losing her new pets."
"Actually she's not losing them," Henry said.
"I talked to Nathan this morning.
He said his parents aren't against having a pet after all."
"Really?" Cole looked surprised.
"But Nathan said they told Nora she couldn't have one!"
"That was a year ago," Henry reminded him.
"They didn't think she was ready to take care of a pet then.
But she's older now.
They said if she promised to be good from now on, she could keep Patches.
And Patches' kittens can stay until someone adopts them."
"Awesome!" Cole said. Then he pointed down the street.
"Here comes Maggie with our money. That's even more awesome!"
Maggie hurried over, carrying a plate covered in foil.
"Hi, guys," she said. "Ready to sell more lemonade?
I'll run inside and get the pitchers."
"First things first," Cole said. "Did you get our fee from Nathan?"
Maggie hesitated. "Um, sort of."
"What do you mean, sort of?" Henry said.
Maggie smiled sheepishly. "Did you notice how adorable those kittens were?"
"Yeah, they were cute," Cole said impatiently. "But where's my money?
Did Nathan pay you or not?"
"He paid me," Maggie said. "But not with money.
I, um, told him I'd take two kittens instead of the five dollars."
"What?" Cole shrieked. "Are you kidding?"
"Sorry," Maggie said quickly.
"I know I should have checked with you guys first. But the kittens are so cute, and they need homes . . .
I just couldn't resist, even if it means waiting longer to start riding lessons."
Cole looked annoyed.
"Okay, you got two kittens for solving the case," he complained.
"What do Henry and I get?"
"You can split our next detective fee, just the two of you," Maggie said. "I promise."
Henry smiled. It hadn't been fair for Maggie to give away their fee without asking.
But if she was willing to give up her share of the next one, she must really want those kittens.
"It's a deal," he said before Cole could respond.
"Great!" Maggie seemed relieved.
"And look, Nathan's mom gave us these to thank us!"
She uncovered the plate. It was full of chocolate chip cookies.
"Yum." That made Cole a little happier.
"Just ask next time, Maggie, okay?"
Maggie nodded. "Sorry."
Meanwhile Henry had spotted Gail and her older sister walking toward them.
"Uh-oh," he said. "I think our first customers of the day are coming.
We'd better get some lemonade."
"Be right back." Maggie dashed into the house and returned a few seconds later carrying two pitchers of lemonade.
By then the girls had reached the lemonade stand.
"Two lemonades please," Gail's sister said.
"We heard you solved another case," Gail added.
"You heard about that already?" Cole looked excited.
The three friends grinned at each other.
Henry was glad that word was spreading about The Lemonade Detectives.
That would bring them more cases.
He couldn't wait to find out what the next one would be!
"Here's your lemonade," Henry said.
He handed a cup of ice-cold lemonade to a teenage girl.
"Please come again," Henry's cousin Maggie added.
"And let us know if you have any mysteries for us to solve."
"Okay." The girl took a sip of her lemonade.
"But nothing mysterious ever happens here in Belltown."
Henry grinned. "That's what you think!" he said.
"The Lemonade Detectives have solved five mysteries so far."
He pointed to two signs on the lemonade stand.
One of the signs was about the lemonade they were selling.
The other sign was about The Lemonade Detective Agency.
Henry, Maggie, and their friend Cole had started the agency a couple of weeks ago.
At first it had been just a lemonade stand.
Maggie had started selling lemonade to earn money for horseback-riding lessons.
Her parents had promised to pay half of her lesson fees, but she had to pay the rest herself.
Maggie's lemonade stand had been a big success from the start.
On her very first day, she'd made a lot of money.
But then the money had disappeared from her cashbox!
Henry and Cole had helped her figure out who had taken it.
After that the three of them had decided to open the detective agency.
The teenage girl looked at the signs.
"Oh right. I heard you helped my neighbor figure out how a groundhog was getting into his garden.
That doesn't sound like a very exciting mystery to me," the girl went on.
"But if anything mysterious happens, I'll let you know."
"Okay," Henry said. "Enjoy your lemonade."
"Thanks." The teenage girl took another sip, and then walked away.
"She's right, you know," Maggie told Henry.
"Our last few mysteries have been kind of boring."
"I know," Henry said. "Finding Mr. Flinn's lost keys wasn't very interesting.
Neither was the groundhog case, or the one about the missing library book.
But we still got paid our detective fee each time, so we shouldn't complain."
"That's true," Maggie agreed.
"If we solve a few more cases, and keep selling lots of lemonade, I'll have enough money for lessons soon."
She dropped the quarter from the teenage girl into the cashbox.
"That's another 25 cents for my horseback-riding fund."
"You mean one-third of 25 cents," Henry corrected her.
"You have to split the money with Cole and me."
Maggie shook her head.
"Cole doesn't get to split the lemonade money when he's not here.
So I get to keep one-half of 25 cents."
"Oops, you're right," Henry said.
"I forgot that Cole has swim-team tryouts again today."
"Why does he want to be on the swim team?" Maggie wondered.
"Hanging out at the lemonade stand seems a lot more fun than swimming laps all day long."
"Cole loves sports," Henry reminded her. "And he's a really good swimmer."
"He's lucky that someone on the team just moved away," Maggie said.
"Otherwise he wouldn't have a chance to try out until next summer."
Henry nodded. "Cole is the youngest kid trying to make the team," he said.
"But it sounds like he did really well on the first day of tryouts.
I bet he'll make the team."
"I know why he's such a good swimmer," Maggie said with a laugh.
"Why?" Henry asked her.
"Because he spends so much time watching his pet frogs swim around their tank!"
Henry grinned. Cole was crazy about reptiles and amphibians.
He had several large tanks in his bedroom. One tank was full of frogs.
Another tank was for his turtles, and a third one held a snake.
Cole took very good care of all his pets.
"Yeah," Henry said, still smiling.
"Frogs are good swimmers, and so is Cole!"
"Hey, here comes Cole now." Maggie pointed down the street.
Henry was surprised to see Cole running toward them from the direction of the town pool.
"I wonder why he's back so soon," Henry said.
"Tryouts just started a few minutes ago. They shouldn't be over for hours."
Maggie shrugged.
"Maybe the coach already told him that he didn't make the team."
"I doubt it," Henry said, still watching Cole.
"I don't think they even started swimming yet today.
Look! Cole's hair isn't wet."
"That's a smart observation, Detective Henry," Maggie said with a laugh.
Cole was closer by now. Henry could see that he was very upset.
"What's wrong?" Henry asked. "Why aren't you at the pool?"
Cole skidded to a stop in front of the lemonade stand.
"I need your help!" he cried.
"Someone dumped a bunch of frogs into the pool right before tryouts started.
And everyone thinks I'm the one who did it!"
"What do you mean, someone dumped frogs in the pool?" Maggie asked.
"I mean just what I said," Cole replied.
"All the swimmers were helping the coach carry some stuff to the pool from his car.
When we got to the pool, we saw the frogs.
About twelve of them were swimming around."
"Are you sure the frogs didn't hop into the pool by themselves?" Henry asked.
Cole nodded. "I'm sure. These aren't the kind of frogs you see around here."
"Okay. If you say so," Maggie said with a shrug. "You're the frog expert."
"That's the problem!" Cole looked more worried than ever.
"A few of the other swimmers know I like frogs.
That's why they think I did it.
But I would never throw a bunch of frogs into pool water.
It's not healthy for them."
"Why not?" Maggie asked. "I thought frogs liked water."
"They do," Cole said. "But pool water has chlorine in it.
That can be bad for them."
"Did you tell everyone that?" Henry asked.
"Yes, but most of them still think I did it," Cole said.
"I need The Lemonade Detectives to help me clear my name!"
"We're on the case!" said Maggie.
Henry and Maggie closed down the lemonade stand.
Then they walked to the pool with Cole.
When they arrived, a bunch of kids were in the pool with nets, still chasing the frogs.
Someone had put buckets of fresh water near the edge of the pool.
Whenever the swimmers caught a frog, they put it into a bucket.
"Are the frogs okay?" Cole called, rushing over and looking into the buckets.
"Do any of them look sick?"
A girl named Daisy looked at him.
She was two years ahead of Henry and Cole in school.
"I think we got them out fast enough," she said.
An older kid named John gave Cole a dirty look.
"Yeah. No thanks to you, frog boy!" he said.
Coach Phillips stepped forward.
He was a cheerful man, who was almost always smiling.
But Henry could see that he wasn't smiling now.
"That's enough," the swim coach told John.
"Everyone is innocent until proven guilty."
"Okay, Coach." John shrugged.
"But everyone knows who the frog lover is around here."
A couple of kids nodded.
Others stared at Cole suspiciously or looked confused.
"Uh-oh," Henry whispered to Maggie. "Cole was right.
He's the main suspect! We'd better start investigating!"
"How are we supposed to figure out who put the frogs in the pool?" Maggie asked.
"We can't check the frogs for fingerprints!"
"Good point," Henry said with a grin.
"But we can split up and start talking to people.
Maybe someone saw what really happened."
"Okay," Maggie said. "I'll go question Daisy."
She walked away. Henry looked around.
Belltown was pretty small, so he knew almost everyone at the pool.
A kid who lived across the street from him was standing in the water.
His name was Arnold, but everyone called him Tiny.
The nickname was a joke because Tiny was the tallest kid in the tenth grade.
"Hi, Tiny," Henry said, walking over.
"Hi, Henry," Tiny said. "Did you come to help us catch these frogs?"
Henry smiled. "Sorry, I just came to watch the tryouts.
So I don't have my swimsuit on."
"That's okay." Tiny looked around the pool.
"I think we got most of them already."
Henry looked around too. He saw two frogs still swimming around.
The rest were already in the buckets.
"Is everyone here trying out for the team?" he asked Tiny.
"Not exactly." Tiny shrugged.
"There are only six spots on the team, and five of them are already taken.
I've been on the team all summer, so I have one of the spots.
The Farley twins, Mary Martinez, and John Miller are already on the team too."
Just then Henry saw a frog swim past. "There's one!" he cried.
Tiny swam after the frog.
He chased it halfway to the other end and finally caught it.
Henry carried a bucket closer. Tiny swam over to him.
"How many people are trying out for the last spot on the team?"
Henry asked as Tiny put the frog in the bucket.
"Four," Tiny said. "Your friend Cole and three other people."
"Wow," Henry said. "Four swimmers trying out for one spot.
That's a lot of competition."
"If you ask me, Cole is the best swimmer of the four," Tiny said.
"He'll probably get the spot."
Just then a young girl walked past.
She was one of the few kids that Henry didn't recognize.
She stopped when she heard what Tiny had just said.
"Don't be so sure!" the girl said, glaring at Tiny.
"Cole definitely won't be getting a spot on the team if I have anything to say about it!"
"Who was that?" Henry asked Tiny as the girl stomped away.
"Lauren," Tiny said.
"She's in college. Coach Phillips hired her to be his assistant coach."
Henry was surprised. "I thought she was a high-school student.
She looks really young."
"That's what Cole said when he met her yesterday," Tiny said.
"I guess Lauren doesn't like being called young.
She got really insulted when he said it, and she's been giving Cole dirty looks ever since."
"Hey, Tiny!" someone called from the other end of the pool.
"There's one last frog over here that we can't catch."
"See you later, Henry," Tiny said. Then he swam away.
Henry returned the frog bucket while he thought about what he'd just learned.
It sounded as if Cole had accidentally insulted Lauren and she was still mad about it.
Could she be angry enough to try to ruin Cole's chances of making the team?
Soon Tiny and the others caught the last frog.
Coach Phillips looked relieved.
"All right, people," he called out.
"Time to get back to tryouts. Everyone in the pool!"
Maggie walked over to Henry.
"Daisy says she didn't see a thing," she reported.
"But she thinks that Cole did it.
Mostly because he put a plastic toad in her lunch once."
"I remember that," Henry said. "Cole loves joking around.
I'm sure that's another reason why some people believe he did this."
Maggie nodded. "Did you find out anything useful?" she asked.
"I was talking to Tiny when the assistant coach walked past . . ."
Henry went on to describe what Lauren had said.
Then he told Maggie what Tiny had said afterward.
"Wow," Maggie said when he finished.
"Lauren must be really sensitive about looking young.
Do you think she was mad enough at Cole to do this?"
"I was wondering the same thing," Henry said.
"But how would she know that Cole liked frogs? She only met him yesterday.
We shouldn't assume it was her until we know more.
Maybe we can talk to other people when the team takes a break."
The two of them sat down to watch as tryouts continued.
The coach had all the swimmers do laps for a while.
Then he told Tiny and the other team members to get out of the pool and rest.
Cole and the other three kids who were trying out had to stay in the water.
The coach asked them to swim all the different strokes.
"Wow. Cole really is a good swimmer," Maggie commented.
"Daisy and Kyle are pretty good too," Henry said.
"But that last kid is terrible," Maggie said.
"Who is he? He looks familiar."
"That's Tommy Miller," Henry said.
"He's one year ahead of Cole and me in school."
Maggie shook her head. "He really stinks.
Why would he try out for the swim team?"
"Maybe it's because his older brother is one of the stars of the team."
Henry looked over at John Miller.
Tommy's older brother was sitting with Tiny and the others.
John was bragging about getting his driver's license soon, when he turned sixteen.
"I guess John got all the swimming talent in the family," Maggie said.
Henry went back to watching Tommy. He was swimming the backstroke.
But by the time he was halfway across the pool, he looked like he was about to drown.
He had to dog paddle to finally get to the other end.
"I just remembered something," Henry said.
"Tommy's parents own the pet store at the mall.
That's where Cole buys food and supplies for his pets."
"So?" Maggie said.
"So Tommy knew about Cole's interest in frogs. Maybe he's trying to frame him."
"Frame him? What does that mean?" Maggie asked.
"It's a detective word," Henry said.
"It's when someone tries to make it look as if someone else committed a crime."
"So you think Tommy framed Cole for the frog prank?"
Maggie looked doubtful. "Why would he do that?"
"Because Cole's such a good swimmer," Henry said.
"And Tommy really wants the spot on the team."
Maggie thought for a second.
"Yeah, but even if Cole got kicked out of tryouts, there's no way Tommy would make the team.
Daisy and Kyle are both better than him too."
Henry realized she was right.
Just then the coach ordered Cole and the others out of the pool for a rest.
All four of them climbed out and hurried toward the chairs where they'd left their towels and sports drinks.
"Maybe Daisy and Kyle should be suspects instead of Tommy," Henry said to Maggie.
"Do you think they knew that Cole likes frogs?"
Before Maggie could answer, there was a loud shriek.
"Help!" Daisy screamed. "I'm being attacked by ants!"
Henry spun around when he heard Daisy scream.
He saw her throw a towel onto the ground.
Tiny black insects were crawling up her arms!
She raced toward the pool and jumped in.
A second later she came up from underwater. "Whew!" Daisy said.
"There was a swarm of ants on my towel!
Luckily I rinsed them off before they could bite me."
Henry hurried over to look at the towel Daisy had dropped.
Sure enough, dozens of ants were crawling all over it!
"That's weird." Cole looked over Henry's shoulder.
"How did those ants get there?"
Henry was wondering the same thing.
He shook off the ants, and then took a closer look at the towel.
It was white, but there was a purple stain on it.
When he sniffed the stain, it smelled sweet, like grape juice.
"What is it?" Maggie asked.
"Daisy must have spilled her sports drink on her towel," Henry said.
"Ants love sweet stuff."
He went over to where Daisy was talking to Coach Phillips.
Henry showed them the stain.
"Did you spill something on your towel earlier?" he asked Daisy.
"It's not my towel," Daisy said.
"I forgot mine, so I borrowed that one from Tiny."
"Let me see that, Henry."
Coach Phillips looked at the towel with an anxious frown.
"I hope someone didn't spill their drink in the locker room.
There will be ants everywhere! I'd better go check."
"I have an extra towel in the office," Lauren told Daisy.
"We'll be right back, everyone."
Coach Phillips, Lauren, and Daisy headed toward the pool building.
"Do you think the ants are connected to the frog prank?" Maggie asked Henry.
"I'm not sure," Henry said. "Let's go ask Tiny about his towel."
Henry and Maggie walked over to Tiny.
"Did you know there was grape drink on that towel you loaned to Daisy?" Maggie demanded.
Tiny shook his head.
"That towel was clean when I put it in my locker this morning.
Maybe Tommy accidentally dragged it in something when he took it out of my locker."
"You mean Tommy was the one who brought the towel to Daisy?" Henry asked.
"Why didn't you get it yourself?"
"I was busy stretching, so John said he'd ask Tommy to get it," Tiny said.
"But I still feel terrible about what happened."
"Maybe Cole isn't the only swimmer that Tommy wanted out of tryouts," Henry murmured to Maggie as they walked away.
"Maybe Tommy is trying to chase away all of his competition, including Daisy!"
"That's the only way he could ever make the team," Maggie said.
"Let's go question him!"
She raced toward Tommy. "Why did you give Daisy that towel?"
Tommy looked confused.
"Because Daisy forgot hers, and Tiny had an extra one," he said.
"How did that grape stuff get on there?" Maggie demanded.
"And all those ants?"
"I don't know," Tommy said.
Henry couldn't tell if Tommy was lying or telling the truth.
Either way Henry was afraid that Maggie's questions might make him mad.
He quickly changed the subject.
"Hey, Tommy," he said. "Why did you decide to try out for the swim team?"
"My parents wanted me to get some exercise this summer," Tommy said.
"I thought it would be fun to swim with my brother.
Too bad I stink at swimming!" He laughed.
Just then John came over to give him some swimming tips.
Henry and Maggie wandered away.
"Do you think Tommy's telling the truth?" Maggie asked.
"I'm not sure," Henry said. "Let's go see what Cole thinks."
Cole was checking on the frogs. "Did you solve the mystery yet?" he asked.
"Not yet," Henry said, keeping his voice low.
"But we have a couple of suspects. One of them is Tommy Miller."
"We think he might be trying to get you kicked out of tryouts," added Maggie.
"That way he'll have a better chance to make the team."
"Tommy?" Cole shook his head. "No way. He's a nice kid.
Plus he's not competitive like his older brother.
Tommy doesn't care if he makes the team or not."
Just then Kyle marched over. He was two years older than Henry and Cole.
"You should go home and take your frogs with you, Cole," Kyle said loudly.
"Fifth-grade nerds don't belong here!
You should have tried out for the junior swim team."
"I'll be in sixth grade in the fall," Cole told him.
"That means I can try out for either team."
Kyle took a sip of the purple sports drink he was holding, and then smirked.
"Oh yeah?" he said. "I just heard Coach Phillips talking to Lauren.
She's trying to talk him into kicking you out of tryouts!"
"What?" Cole exclaimed, staring at Kyle.
"No way!" Maggie said.
"Does Lauren really want Coach Phillips to kick Cole out of tryouts?"
"That's what I just said," Kyle said with another smirk.
He took one more sip of his sports drink, and then wandered away.
Cole looked upset. "I have to go talk to the coach!
I have to beg him to give me another chance!"
"Wait a minute, Cole," said Henry.
"Everyone knows that Kyle likes to cause trouble.
What if he's just trying to make you worry?"
Maggie nodded.
"He's probably upset because you're doing better than him in the tryouts.
He could be another one of our suspects!"
"She's right," Henry said.
"Did you notice that Kyle was sipping a sports drink?
I'm pretty sure it was grape."
"Really?" Maggie said. "That proves it!
Kyle must have poured the grape drink on the towel.
Then he dragged it through an anthill to try to scare Daisy away.
He probably framed Cole for the frogs too!"
Cole shrugged. "I guess it's possible.
Kyle really wants the spot on the team.
He's been teasing me all day, saying I'm too young and stuff like that."
"Case closed!" Maggie exclaimed. "Let's go tell the coach!"
"Wait," Henry said. As usual Maggie was rushing things.
"The case isn't closed yet. We don't know for sure that Kyle did it.
What if he's telling the truth about what he heard?
Lauren was already one of our suspects.
Maybe she wants to get Cole kicked out because he insulted her yesterday."
Cole made a face.
"Yeah, my big mouth sure got me in trouble with her," he admitted.
"I tried to apologize, but she wouldn't listen."
"Maybe we should go ask Coach Phillips if what Kyle said is true," Henry said.
"If it is, then Lauren should be our main suspect.
Otherwise it should be Kyle."
Cole looked around the pool area for the coach.
"He must still be inside. Let's go!"
Henry, Cole, and Maggie headed toward the pool building.
Just as they reached the door, Lauren came out with Daisy.
Lauren saw Cole and frowned.
"Where are you going?" she demanded.
"Inside," Cole said. "We need to talk to the coach."
"You don't have time right now," Lauren said.
"I'm in charge until Coach Phillips comes back outside.
And I want everyone to run laps around the pool building. Now!"
She raised her voice for the last part so everyone could hear.
A few of the swimmers groaned.
But she ordered them to put on their sneakers and start running.
Henry and Maggie watched as the swimmers disappeared behind the pool building.
Lauren jogged away with them, leaving the pool area deserted.
"It makes me feel hot just watching people jog in this weather," Maggie said.
"Let's go stand in the shade."
"Okay." Henry followed her around the corner of the building.
There was shade there from some large trees, and they could see some walking trails too.
Henry tried to glance back at the pool.
But he couldn't see it from where they were standing.
"Lauren seems really mad at Cole," he said.
"She made everyone jog so he couldn't go inside and talk to the coach.
Do you think she guessed that we suspect her?"
"Maybe," Maggie said. "But I still think Kyle could be the bad guy.
He really wants to get on the team.
Cole and Daisy are the only two people who might stop him.
And the two pranks today were aimed at them."
"We shouldn't forget about Tommy though," Henry said.
"He was the one who gave Daisy that towel.
That means he's still a suspect too."
Maggie looked doubtful. "Cole thinks it couldn't be Tommy."
Henry was about to answer when he heard a shout. It came from near the pool.
"That sounded like Coach Phillips!" he said. "Let's go!"
Around the corner the coach was staring into the pool.
A few of the joggers, including Cole, had made it back to the building by then.
"What's wrong, Coach?" Cole called.
Coach Phillips pointed to the water. "The frogs!" he exclaimed.
"They're in the pool again!"
Henry gasped when he saw the buckets tipped over at the edge of the pool.
The rest of the joggers appeared around the corner.
When they saw what had happened, everyone started talking at once.
"Quiet!" the coach hollered. "I want to know who did this!"
