Nobody said a word.
Lauren hurried toward the edge of the pool and picked up something on the ground near the buckets.
"Look!" she cried. "Whoever did it left a pair of flip-flops behind."
She held up two blue-and-white flip-flops. Cole let out a gasp.
"Those are mine!" he blurted out.
Henry stared at Cole in shock. So did everyone else.
"Your flip-flops were at the scene of the crime," Kyle said, pointing at Cole.
"That means you dumped the frogs back in the water!"
John nodded. "I bet he did it the first time too."
"I knew it!" Lauren muttered.
Henry didn't know what to think. Those flip-flops were a big clue.
Could Cole be the culprit? After all, Cole did love a good joke.
But Cole was shaking his head, looking more upset than ever.
"I didn't do it!" he told Coach Phillips. "I swear!"
That brought Henry back to his senses.
Cole might be a joker, but he wasn't a liar.
If Cole said he was innocent, then Henry believed him.
But he could tell most of the others didn't.
Even Coach Phillips had a doubtful frown on his face.
"We'll talk about it later," the coach said.
"First we'd better get those frogs rounded up again."
The swimmers all jumped in the pool and started catching frogs.
Henry and Maggie watched.
"This doesn't look good for Cole," Maggie whispered.
"I know," Henry whispered back.
"If we don't solve this mystery fast, Cole will never make the swim team!"
"Someone must have put Cole's flip-flops by the buckets so he'd get the blame," Maggie said.
"Who could have done that?"
"I don't know."
Henry tried to remember who had been near the pool when he and Maggie had returned.
The coach had been there of course.
So had a few of the faster joggers, including Cole.
But Henry couldn't remember who else was in the fast group.
Maggie was staring at Lauren.
The assistant coach was watching the swimmers retrieve the frogs.
"Lauren was the one who spotted the flip-flops," Maggie said.
"Maybe that's because she was the one who put them there."
"Maybe," Henry agreed.
"Let's go talk to her. But let me ask most of the questions, okay?
We don't want her to know we're suspicious of her."
Maggie frowned. But she nodded. "Okay," she said.
They walked over to Lauren. "Hi," Henry said.
"I'm Henry, and this is my cousin Maggie."
"Nice to meet you. I'm Lauren," Lauren said.
"Are you here to try out for the team?
Because we usually recommend wearing a swimsuit."
Henry laughed. "No, we're just here to watch our friends try out."
"You didn't bring your pet frogs with you, did you?" Lauren asked, smiling a little.
Henry's dad was a reporter who had a lot of experience interviewing people.
Henry suddenly remembered his dad's advice: A good way to start an interview is to ask people about themselves.
"We heard you're a student at Bellville College," Henry said to Lauren.
"Do you like it there?"
"Sure, it's great," Lauren said. "I've been there for three years.
I'll graduate next spring."
"Really?" Maggie blurted out. "Wow, you look much younger than that!"
Lauren's friendly expression instantly changed to a frown.
"Excuse me," she snapped. "I have work to do."
Henry sighed as Lauren stomped away.
"You already knew she was sensitive about looking young," he said to Maggie.
"Why did you have to mention it?"
"Sorry." Maggie shrugged. "I couldn't help it."
Henry knew better than to get annoyed at his cousin.
She had a habit of saying whatever was on her mind without thinking about it first.
"Forget about it," he murmured, thinking hard.
Maggie was thinking too. "Lauren is so sensitive about her age.
She's probably still mad at Cole.
Maybe even mad enough to try to get him kicked out of tryouts!"
"Right," agreed Henry. "Let's go see what Cole thinks."
Cole was putting a frog into one of the buckets.
Henry and Maggie hurried to Cole before he could swim away.
Henry bent down to talk to him. "We were just talking to Lauren.
We think she might still be mad at you."
"That makes her our top suspect for everything, including dumping the frogs again," Maggie added.
"Especially since she was the one who spotted your flip-flops."
Cole shook his head.
"She might have done the earlier stuff," he said.
"But I know she didn't tip over the buckets."
"How can you be so sure?" Henry asked.
"She was near me the whole time we were jogging," Cole said.
"She ran right behind me, yelling at me to go faster.
She only slowed down to check on the others when I was almost all the way around the building."
"Are you sure?" Maggie asked.
Cole nodded. "Lauren's definitely still mad at me," he said with a sigh.
"But she's definitely not the one who dumped those frogs back in the pool."
"So Lauren wasn't the one who dumped the frogs back in the pool," Maggie said.
"But that doesn't mean she didn't do the other stuff.
Like put the frogs in the pool the first time. Or put ants on Daisy's towel."
"True," Henry agreed.
"But why would she do that to Daisy?
Did Daisy say something about her looking young too?"
"I don't think so," Cole said.
"Then Lauren probably didn't do the ant prank either," Henry said.
"Let's talk about our other suspects."
"You mean Kyle and Tommy?" Maggie asked.
"I still don't think Tommy did it," Cole said. "He's my friend."
"Okay," Henry said. "But he does have a good motive.
If you get kicked out of tryouts, he has a better chance of making the team."
"It didn't seem like he really cares about making the team," Maggie said.
"Don't forget that his brother is a star," Henry said.
"What if Tommy cares more about the team than he's showing?
And it would be easy for him to get the frogs from his parents' pet store."
Maggie's eyes lit up. "Plus Tommy was the one who gave Daisy that towel.
He might have poured grape drink on it, and then dragged it through an anthill."
"That doesn't sound like something Tommy would do," Cole said.
"Aren't there any other suspects?"
"Sure," Henry said.
"The other two people with good motives are Kyle and Daisy."
"Daisy?" Maggie said. "But she's the one who got attacked by ants!"
"She could have set that up herself," Henry said.
"That way nobody would suspect her of the frog prank."
"Maybe." Cole looked unsure. "It doesn't seem very likely though.
She almost got bitten. And ant bites really hurt."
Just then Lauren wandered past. "Hey," she said, pointing at Cole.
"Aren't you supposed to be the frog expert around here?"
He nodded.
"Then help catch those frogs!"
"Okay." Cole waved to his friends and swam away.
"I guess Lauren knows that Cole likes frogs," Maggie said to Henry.
"Are you sure she's not the culprit?"
Maggie's voice was pretty loud.
Henry didn't want everyone to hear them talking, so he led her over to the playground.
The two of them sat down on the swings.
"I'm pretty sure," Henry told Maggie.
"Lauren had no reason to make those ants swarm Daisy."
"What if the ant prank was just a coincidence?" Maggie asked.
"Maybe Tiny spilled grape juice on his towel, and then Tommy dragged it through an anthill without noticing."
"It's possible," Henry said. "But I'm still pretty sure about Lauren.
She couldn't have dumped the frog buckets while she was jogging behind the pool building."
"I guess that's true." Maggie said.
"It had to be one of the joggers who finished first.
Who's the fastest runner out of our suspects?"
"Probably Kyle," Henry said. "He was on the track team at school."
"And we saw him with a grape sports drink," Maggie said.
"Plus we know he really wants the spot on the swim team.
He has to be the culprit!"
"We have to be able to prove it's Kyle," Henry reminded her.
"Let's go talk to him and see what we can find out."
They found Kyle chasing a frog in the pool.
"Hi, Kyle," Henry greeted him.
"Can you believe those frogs got in the water again?"
"I can't believe it!" Kyle said. "Your friend Cole is a troublemaker.
I hope the coach kicks him out this time!"
Maggie scowled. "Cole didn't do it!"
"That's not what everybody else says."
Kyle grinned and puffed out his chest.
"Once Cole's gone, that spot on the team will be all mine!"
Henry traded a look with Maggie.
He could tell they were thinking the same thing. Kyle sounded guilty!
"You're a chicken, Kyle!" Maggie said angrily.
"You're afraid Cole will beat you."
"No way," Kyle said. "I'm not afraid of anybody!
Having Cole out of the way just makes it easier.
Maybe he should take some of these frogs home with him so they can teach him how to swim."
Kyle laughed loudly, as if that was the funniest thing anyone had ever said.
But Henry frowned.
"What do you mean?" he asked Kyle. "Cole already has a bunch of pet frogs."
"Really?" Kyle looked surprised.
"So that's why John called Cole 'frog boy.'"
Henry was still watching Kyle closely. "You didn't know that Cole has frogs?"
Kyle shrugged. "I don't pay much attention to fifth-grade nerds," he said.
"Speaking of which, why am I standing here talking to you?"
He smirked and then swam away.
"What a jerk," Maggie muttered.
"He might be a jerk," Henry said. "But he's definitely not our culprit."
"What are you talking about?" Maggie asked Henry in surprise.
"I thought we agreed that Kyle was our top suspect."
"He was," Henry said. "But he's not anymore.
He just told us that he didn't know Cole was interested in frogs.
That means he wouldn't know that Cole would be blamed for the prank!"
"I didn't think of that," Maggie said.
"Plus it would be stupid for Kyle to use grape sports drink for the ant prank," Henry added.
"Everyone saw him drinking it all day."
Maggie shrugged. "Maybe he's not very bright.
Or maybe he was lying about not knowing Cole liked frogs."
"Maybe," Henry said. "But I don't think so.
We'd better check out our other suspects. Starting with Tommy.
He definitely knew Cole liked frogs because of his parents' pet store.
Plus Tommy could have gotten the frogs there."
"Sure," Maggie said.
"But Cole isn't the only one who's a better swimmer than Tommy.
Why didn't Tommy try to ruin Daisy and Kyle's chances too?"
"Maybe that's why Tommy did the ant prank," Henry said.
"He was trying to get rid of the other two swimmers that way.
If Daisy got bitten by ants, she might not want to try out anymore.
And using grape sports drink meant Kyle might get the blame."
Maggie gasped. "Henry, you're a genius!" she exclaimed.
"That makes perfect sense! Let's go tell the coach!"
"Hold on," Henry said. "It's just a theory. We haven't proven anything yet."
"How are we going to prove it?" Maggie asked.
"I'm not sure yet. Let's go talk to Tommy."
Henry looked over at the pool.
Most of the swimmers were chasing the last few frogs.
Lauren was watching them.
Coach Phillips seemed to be counting the frogs that were already in the buckets.
But Tommy was nowhere in sight.
"Where is he?" Maggie wondered.
"I don't know," Henry said. "But there's his brother John.
Let's go ask him if he knows where Tommy is."
John was climbing out of the pool. He had an annoyed expression on his face.
Henry wondered if that was because tryouts had been disrupted again.
Everyone in town knew that John was a very talented swimmer.
"Hi, John," Henry said. "We're looking for your brother. Where did he go?"
"That's a good question." John looked more annoyed than ever.
"I was just looking for him myself."
"Why?" Maggie asked.
"Tryouts will start again in a few minutes, and he needs all the practice he can get," John said.
"Tommy isn't taking these tryouts very seriously."
Then he stomped away.
Maggie watched him go. "John sounded mad," she said.
"And did you hear what he said about Tommy?
Maybe John suspects his brother of causing all the trouble!"
Henry shrugged. "Brothers get mad at each other all the time.
John is probably just embarrassed because his brother is a terrible swimmer."
"Yeah, you're probably right," Maggie agreed.
Henry noticed Cole putting another frog in one of the buckets.
Most of the other swimmers were climbing out of the pool and grabbing their towels.
"It looks like they caught all the frogs," Henry said.
"We'd better hurry if we want to talk to Tommy before tryouts start again."
"There's Daisy. Let's ask her if she's seen him," Maggie said.
"I saw Tommy heading toward the pool building a few minutes ago," Daisy told them a second later.
"He probably went inside to use the bathroom."
"Thanks," Henry said. He wondered if he should ask Daisy more questions.
She was still a suspect too. "Hey, Daisy," he said.
"When Lauren made you jog, did you make it around the building first?"
Daisy smiled. "Not this time," she said.
"At first I was keeping up with Cole, Kyle, and John.
But then I saw a pretty flower growing beside the running trail, and I stopped to look at it.
I thought I might want to come back and paint it later.
So I was one of the last ones to make it back."
"Oh." Henry remembered that Daisy liked art.
He'd seen some of her paintings displayed at school.
Daisy walked away.
"Why were you asking her about jogging?" Maggie asked Henry.
"I thought we were in a hurry to talk to Tommy."
"I'm still trying to figure out who dumped those frogs the second time," Henry said.
"It had to be the first person who got back from that jog.
So Daisy's probably not our culprit."
"I could have told you that!" Maggie rolled her eyes.
"Our top suspect is Tommy now, remember?"
"Okay. Let's go find him."
Before they could move, Henry and Maggie heard an angry howl.
"Hey!" Kyle yelled. "Someone poured paint in my gym bag!"
"Let's go!" Henry said to Maggie.
Without waiting for her, he rushed over to Kyle.
Coach Phillips was hurrying toward him too.
Everyone else had stopped whatever they were doing and turned to stare.
"What happened?" Henry asked when he reached Kyle.
Kyle's large blue gym bag was sitting on a chair near the pool.
Its zipper was halfway open.
When Henry looked down into the opening, he saw a puddle of green.
The green paint was all over Kyle's sneakers, T-shirt, and other belongings.
"All my stuff is ruined!" Kyle complained.
The coach reached them.
"This is outrageous!" he exclaimed as he looked into Kyle's bag.
Then he spun around. "Someone had better confess right now!
Otherwise I'm going to cancel these tryouts!"
"Oh no!" Daisy exclaimed.
Kyle glared at Cole, who was standing a short distance away.
"It was him!" he said, pointing.
"Everyone knows he's the one who dumped those frogs in the pool.
He must have done this too!
He's afraid I'll beat him for that spot on the team!"
"Cole didn't do anything!" Maggie said.
"You probably put that paint there yourself, Kyle!
If there's any paint in your bag, that is."
Henry realized that nobody could see the paint except for him, Kyle, and the coach.
"There's really paint in here, Maggie," he said.
"The only question is how it got there."
"Yes," Coach Phillips agreed.
"And I want an answer to that question right now!
I also want to know who brought those frogs to the pool."
Just then Tommy came out of the pool building.
When he saw everyone staring at Kyle, he looked confused.
"What's going on?" he asked, hurrying over.
"That's a very good question," Coach Phillips said.
"We're trying to figure out who's responsible for all of today's pranks."
"I know the answer," Maggie declared. She pointed at Tommy. "He did it!"
"What?" Tommy exclaimed.
Henry winced. He thought Tommy was probably the culprit too.
But they still had no way to prove it.
Why did Maggie have to have such a big mouth?
John looked angry.
"How dare you accuse my brother of something like that!" he yelled at Maggie.
"Tommy didn't have anything to do with this!"
Maggie didn't back down, even though John was a lot older.
"That's not what we think!" Maggie yelled back. "Right, Henry?"
"I don't understand," Tommy said, looking confused.
"What happened? Are the frogs in the pool again?"
"No," Tiny told him. "Someone poured paint in Kyle's bag."
"You want to make everyone think that Cole did all these pranks," Maggie went on.
"How did you do it?"
"That's ridiculous." John scowled.
"It was Cole. Everyone knows he has pet frogs."
"Right!" Lauren jumped in.
"You probably poured that green paint in Kyle's bag too," John went on.
He looked around. "Or maybe it was Daisy. Everyone knows she likes to paint!"
"What?" Daisy cried. "I didn't do anything!"
"And like I keep telling everyone, I didn't put those frogs in the pool!" Cole added.
"I would never do something like that.
Pool water isn't good for frogs!"
Everyone started yelling at once.
Maggie was yelling at Coach Phillips about evidence.
John was yelling that Tommy was innocent.
Kyle was yelling about his bag being ruined.
Cole and Daisy were yelling that they hadn't done anything wrong.
Everyone else was yelling out questions.
But Henry wasn't yelling. He was thinking.
Something someone had just said didn't make sense.
That was a clue. A big one!
Suddenly he realized who was behind all the trouble.
"Hold on," he said. "I know who did this."
Nobody heard him. Everyone else was still yelling.
So Henry stuck his fingers in his mouth and let out a loud whistle.
Everyone fell silent for a second. They all turned to look at Henry.
"I know who did this," he said again.
"You do?" Maggie asked.
"Of course he does," Kyle said. "Henry is friends with Cole.
He probably even helped Cole.
Why else would he hang around the pool all day?"
"Yeah." John rolled his eyes. "Why are we even listening to him?
He doesn't know anything."
"He might," Daisy said. "Haven't you heard about The Lemonade Detectives?
Henry and his friends helped my neighbor find his lost keys last week."
"Really?" Tiny asked. "That's cool. Can you guys find my lost cell phone?"
"Quiet!" Coach Phillips shouted.
"Henry, do you really know something about all this?"
Henry nodded. "Cole didn't have anything to do with the pranks," he said.
"Neither did Daisy or Kyle or Tommy."
"Then who did it?" Maggie asked.
Henry looked over at Tommy's brother. "It was John."
"How dare you accuse me!" John exclaimed as everyone else gasped.
"You can't prove anything!"
"I can't prove you dumped those frogs," Henry said.
"But I know you poured the paint in Kyle's bag.
Kyle, Coach Phillips, and I were the only ones who looked at the paint.
But you just said it was green paint.
How would you know that unless you poured it in there yourself?"
Daisy gasped. "He did say it was green!"
"That was just a lucky guess," John protested.
"Daisy is always painting pictures of trees and stuff.
I figured she'd use green paint!"
But the coach was frowning.
"Did you have anything to do with those frogs, John?" he asked.
"His parents own a pet store," Tiny spoke up.
"I bet he got the frogs there and dumped them in the pool when we weren't looking!"
"I just remembered something," Cole said. "John was the fastest jogger.
He got back to the pool before the rest of us."
"I remember that too," Kyle said. "Cole and I got there next.
But it took us a few more minutes than John.
He had plenty of time to dump the frogs back in the water."
"And place my flip-flops near the buckets," Cole added.
Tommy stared at his brother.
"Is that why you said you'd go inside and get Tiny's towel for Daisy, John?"
"Aha!" Henry said. "So John was behind the ant trick too!"
Finally John hid his face in his hands.
"Okay, you're right. It was all me!" he blurted out.
"I stained the towel and dragged it through an anthill.
Then I folded it so nobody would notice the ants until Daisy used the towel.
I dumped the frogs in the pool too. I'm sorry.
I thought if I got rid of everyone else, Tommy might make the team."
Tommy stared at John. "Why would you do that?
You know I don't care much about swimming."
"If you don't make the swim team, Mom and Dad will let you take tennis lessons instead," John said.
"I heard them talking about how expensive that is.
They might not have enough money to buy me a car for my birthday!"
"Wow," Maggie whispered to Henry. "John had a motive we didn't know about!"
The coach looked very serious. "Come with me, John," he said.
"We'd better call your parents."
The next day Maggie and Henry were at the lemonade stand.
"The last day of tryouts is almost over," Maggie said.
"I wonder if Cole made the team."
Suddenly they heard a shout.
"That sounds like Cole," Henry said.
Cole raced toward them, grinning. "I made it!" he cried.
"I'm on the swim team!"
"Congratulations!" Henry and Maggie exclaimed.
They each gave him a high five.
"Kyle must be mad that you got the spot," Maggie said.
"Nope," Cole said. "He made it too!
There was an extra spot after Coach Phillips kicked John off the team."
"Then Daisy must be mad," Maggie said.
Cole shrugged. "Not really.
Her parents said she could take horseback-riding lessons instead."
"What about Lauren?" Maggie asked next.
"Is she mad that you made the team?"
"Not anymore," Cole said. "I apologized again for saying she looked young.
This time she listened."
"That's great," Henry said.
"Another great thing happened," Cole went on.
"John's parents gave me the frogs John brought to the pool!
They wanted to apologize for John trying to get me in trouble.
They even gave me free frog food for one month!"
"That's really generous," Henry said.
Cole put his hand in his pocket and pulled out a five-dollar bill.
"I almost forgot. Coach Phillips was really grateful that The Lemonade Detectives solved the mystery.
He offered to pay our detective fee."
Maggie looked away for a second. Then she looked back at Cole.
"You didn't really do much to solve the case.
Plus you got all those free frogs.
So Henry and I should just split the money between the two of us."
"What?" Cole protested. "That's not fair!"
"The Lemonade Detectives are a team, Maggie," Henry reminded her.
"But I've almost got enough money to start horseback-riding lessons!" Maggie argued.
"I need money too!" said Cole.
While they were arguing, a man walked over.
"Would you like to buy some lemonade?" Henry asked.
"No, thanks," the man said.
"My son Kyle told me you three are pretty good detectives."
"That's right," Maggie said. "Do you have a case for us?"
The man sighed.
"Yes. My wife's birthday is this weekend, and I forgot where I hid her gift."
Henry smiled.
Finding a lost birthday gift wasn't the most exciting case in the world.
But that didn't matter.
The Lemonade Detectives solved all mysteries, large or small!
"Here, kitties," Henry said. "Fetch!"
He tossed a cat toy across the family room.
Two kittens ran over and pounced on it.
Henry laughed as the tiny cats batted the toy under the sofa.
Henry was at his aunt and uncle's house.
They lived next door to him and his parents.
It was a nice summer day, and the two families were having a barbecue in the backyard.
"The kittens are cute, Ellen," Henry's mother said as she picked up a plate of hot dogs in the kitchen.
Henry's aunt Ellen sighed. "Yes, they are," she said.
"But they get into everything! I'll be glad when they're a little older."
One of the kittens started rolling on the rug.
The other one jumped onto the sofa. Henry smiled as he watched them.
They were really playful! The kittens belonged to his cousin Maggie.
She was nine years old, two years younger than Henry.
"Should we head outside?" Henry's father asked.
"I could start grilling the food while we wait for Uncle Bruce and Maggie to get home."
Henry's father and Uncle Bruce both loved to cook on Uncle Bruce's fancy grill.
Whenever the families had a barbecue together, the two dads did most of the cooking.
"Good idea," Henry told his father. "I'm hungry!"
"Henry, would you please put the kittens in Maggie's room before we go outside?" Aunt Ellen asked.
"They can't get into too much trouble there.
All her clothes are already covered in cat hair!"
"Sure," Henry said. He scooped up one kitten in each hand.
They wriggled and meowed, trying to escape.
But soon they were safely shut inside Maggie's bedroom.
Henry headed outside.
His parents and Aunt Ellen were setting food on the picnic table.
They were having hot dogs and hamburgers, corn on the cob, and Henry's favorite—watermelon.
"I hope Maggie gets home from her riding lesson soon," Henry's father said as he walked over to the grill.
"I want some of her delicious lemonade."
"Watch out, Dad," Henry joked. "She'll probably charge you 25 cents per cup!"
Everyone chuckled.
Maggie had started a lemonade stand a few weeks ago to earn money for horseback-riding lessons.
Her parents had told her they would pay half the lesson fees if she paid the other half herself.
"I wonder what's taking them so long," Aunt Ellen said, looking at her watch.
"Bruce left to pick Maggie up from the barn almost an hour ago.
They should be home by now."
"Uh-oh," Henry's dad joked.
"Sounds like a mystery for The Lemonade Detectives!"
Henry grinned.
A few weeks ago, Maggie, Henry, and their friend, Cole, had started The Lemonade Detective agency.
They'd already solved quite a few cases.
Some cases were interesting, like figuring out who'd dumped frogs into the town pool.
Other cases were kind of boring, like finding people's lost keys or library books.
But so far The Lemonade Detectives had solved them all.
They were even making money, which was helping to pay for Maggie's horseback-riding lessons.
"That's not much of a mystery, Dad," Henry said.
"We already know that Maggie loves being at the barn.
We also know that she's really talkative.
She's probably giving Uncle Bruce a tour and making him meet all the horses before they leave."
"But I thought this was her third riding lesson," Henry's father said.
"Hasn't Uncle Bruce been to the barn before?"
"Yes," Henry replied with a shrug.
"But that wouldn't stop Maggie from dragging him all over the place!"
Aunt Ellen smiled. "Good detective work, Henry," she said.
"If you're right, will we owe you five dollars for your detective fee?"
"No," Henry said with a laugh. "I'll give you the family discount.
Just don't tell Maggie!"
"It's nice that Maggie is enjoying her lessons," Henry's father said.
"She worked so hard to earn the money for them."
"Yes, she's definitely enjoying them," Aunt Ellen said.
"I think she'd move into the barn if we'd let her!"
Henry grinned. "It's easy to imagine Maggie sleeping in a stall like a horse," he said.
"But I can't imagine her eating hay. She doesn't even like salad!"
Just then the back door swung open.
Maggie came stomping into the backyard, still dressed in her riding clothes.
Her face was bright red, and she did not look happy.
"There's a rotten thief at the barn!" she cried. She pointed at Henry.
"And I need the other Lemonade Detectives to help me figure out who it is!"
"A thief at the barn?" Henry said. "What are you talking about, Maggie?"
By now Maggie's father, Henry's uncle Bruce, had come into the backyard.
"There's no need to be so dramatic, Maggie," he said with a sigh.
"Mom and I have talked to you before about this.
You need to be more careful with your things."
"But I was being careful!" Maggie exclaimed.
"I left the check on my bag, right on top of my sandals.
It was definitely there when I led my pony outside for our lesson.
But when I got back, the check was gone!"
"Wait a minute," Aunt Ellen said.
"Are you saying you lost the check we wrote for today's lesson?"
"Don't worry, I wrote another one," Uncle Bruce told his wife.
"And I called the bank to cancel the first check."
"Oh, Maggie." Aunt Ellen shook her head.
"I can't believe you were so careless, especially after what happened last week."
Henry was surprised. Maggie could be careless about some things.
But she was really careful with her money.
"What happened last week?" he asked.
"Maggie lost a few other things at the barn," Uncle Bruce said.
"Oh dear," Henry's mother said.
"I didn't lose anything!" Maggie protested.
"Someone has been stealing things!"
"Really? What else disappeared?" Henry asked.
"At my first lesson, I took off my charm bracelet and left it in the barn," Maggie said.
"I didn't want to lose it while I was riding.
When I came back inside after my lesson, it was gone!"
"I don't know why you were so worried about losing it," her mother said.
"You always let those kittens of yours use it as a cat toy!"
Maggie frowned. "That's different. The kittens just bat it around.
I always know where it is."
"Did anything else disappear?" Henry asked.
He was already thinking like a detective.
The first thing a good detective needed to do was find out the facts of the case.
Maggie nodded. "At my second lesson, my brand-new horse grooming brush disappeared," she said.
"It happened the same way.
It was in the barn when I went outside for my lesson, but gone when I got back."
"Don't forget about your gloves," her father said.
"Oh, right," Maggie said.
"I didn't wear my riding gloves today because it was so hot.
I left them with my stuff in the barn.
Whoever took that check must have taken the gloves too."
"Maggie!" Aunt Ellen looked shocked. "Those gloves were expensive!"
"Everything about horseback riding is expensive," Uncle Bruce agreed.
"We can't afford to keep replacing things."
Henry could tell that Maggie's parents thought she'd lost all those things.
But he wasn't so sure. Maggie was too careful with money to misplace a check.
She was so excited about riding that he couldn't believe she'd lose a horse brush or her riding gloves.
And he knew she loved that charm bracelet.
"Is anyone allowed inside the barn while there's a lesson outside?" he asked Maggie.
"Sure, I guess so," Maggie said with a shrug.
"I mean, they don't close the doors or anything.
Any rotten thief could just walk in." She clenched her fists.
"I can't believe someone is doing this to me!"
She sounded so dramatic again that all the adults looked at each other.
But Maggie's words made Henry think of another question.
"Has anything else disappeared?" he asked her.
"I mean, anything belonging to other people. Or is it only your stuff?"
"How should I know?" Maggie frowned. "That's what I need you to find out!
Dad made me leave the barn before I could investigate."
Uncle Bruce shook his head.
"We were already late for this barbecue," he said.
"Besides, I don't think there's a mystery here.
It just means that you have to be more careful with your things."
"That's right," Aunt Ellen said.
"I had to pull your favorite horse T-shirt out from under your desk this morning.
The kittens were using it as a bed. It was absolutely covered in cat hair."
Henry's mother cleared her throat.
"Should we eat? Everything smells delicious, and I'm hungry," she said.
"Good idea, Susan," Uncle Bruce agreed.
"Go sit down at the picnic table, everybody.
I'll help Kevin bring the food over from the grill."
The adults were obviously ready to change the subject.
But later, while everyone was eating, Maggie was still thinking about her missing things.
"I didn't lose my stuff at the barn!" she said loudly.
"Somebody stole it! And The Lemonade Detectives will figure out who it was!"
Aunt Ellen glanced up from her corn on the cob.
"I hope so, Maggie," she said.
"Because if this keeps happening, you might not be able to keep riding."
"Ah-choo!" Cole sneezed.
"Bless you," Henry said.
"Thanks." Cole sniffed. "I'm allergic to cats."
It was two days after the family barbecue.
Henry was in the car with Cole and Maggie.
Uncle Bruce was driving them to the barn.
Maggie had another riding lesson, and the boys were going along to investigate the mystery of her missing stuff.
"Sorry, Cole," Uncle Bruce said. "Maggie's kittens have never been in the car.
But their hair gets all over everything, especially Maggie's clothes."
"At least the car doesn't smell like horses," Henry told Cole with a smile.
"Uncle Bruce makes Maggie put on her riding boots at the barn."
He pointed to a bag on the seat beside Maggie.
Her boots and socks were inside, along with her helmet and other riding gear.
Cole was the first one out of the car when they reached the barn.
"Fresh air!" he cried happily. "I can breathe again!"
Maggie rolled her eyes. "Don't get too excited.
There's a barn cat who lives here. Look, there she is."
She pointed to a cat who was sleeping in the sun on top of a hay bale.
"That's okay," Cole said. "I don't usually sneeze when a cat is outside."
They waved good-bye to Maggie's dad and hurried into the barn.
"The pony I ride is over here," Maggie said. "His name is Spot."
She stopped in front of a horse stall and set down her bag.
A pony looked out at them. When Maggie patted him, he nibbled on her hair.
Maggie giggled and gently pushed his head away. "Stop that, Spot!"
Henry heard a bark. A dog came running toward them. His tail was wagging.
A girl Henry didn't recognize came running too. "Come back here, Spot!"
"Hey! This dog has the same name as Maggie's pony!" Cole exclaimed.
He stooped to pat the dog. Cole wasn't allergic to dogs, just cats.
Maggie nodded. "Everyone calls the pony Big Spot and the dog Little Spot," she explained.
"Little Spot belongs to Eleanor.
She's one of the other riders in my group lesson."
By now Eleanor had reached them. "Hi," she said breathlessly.
"Sorry about that. But Little Spot is friendly."
"We don't mind," Cole said. "He's cute."
"Thanks." Eleanor picked up Little Spot. "See you later.
I need to get my pony ready."
She hurried off.
"Shouldn't you be getting Big Spot ready?" Cole asked Maggie.
"I want to show you around the barn first," Maggie said.
"That way you can start investigating."
"Good idea," Henry agreed.
He and Cole followed Maggie down the aisle.
A horse or pony looked out of each stall they passed.
Then they saw a pony standing in the aisle.
A boy was brushing it while a teenage girl watched.
The girl was holding a pitchfork.
"You're not doing that right, Zach," she complained.
"You're supposed to move the brush in circles."
"Leave me alone, Jill," the boy said.
Henry recognized them from his neighborhood.
Zach was in Maggie's class at school. Jill was Zach's older sister.
She and her friend Ashley sometimes came to the lemonade stand.
"Hi, Zach," Henry said. "I didn't know you rode horses."
"I just started." Zach frowned.
"My parents are making me because my sister has a dumb part-time job here."
"You'd have fun if you had a better attitude," Jill told him.
Just then a woman walked toward them.
"Did you finish cleaning the stalls, Jill?" she asked.
"Not yet, Ms. Wood." Jill hurried off to finish her chores.
Maggie introduced Henry and Cole to Ms. Wood.
"She owns the barn and teaches all the lessons," Maggie explained.
Ms. Wood smiled. "Nice to meet you, boys," she said.
"Maggie, it's time to get Big Spot ready.
And you need to change into your riding boots.
It's not safe to wear sandals in the barn."
"Sorry, I was just about to do that," Maggie said. "Come on, you guys."
They headed back down the aisle. On the way, they passed another girl.
Henry recognized her too.
Her name was Daisy, and she was two years ahead of him at school.
"Hi, Maggie," Daisy said. "Am I late for our lesson?"
"Not yet," Maggie told her. "But you'd better hurry."
Daisy rushed away. "I didn't know Daisy was a rider," Cole said.
"She started taking lessons at the same time I did," Maggie explained.
"How many people are in your lesson?" Henry asked.
"You just met them all," Maggie said. "It's Daisy, Zach, Eleanor, and me."
Henry nodded. So far he hadn't seen anything suspicious.
But he wanted to keep track of all the possible suspects.
They turned the corner and saw Big Spot's stall.
Maggie hurried to her bag and pulled out her riding boots.
"Oh no," she moaned. "One of my socks is missing!"
"Are you sure your sock is gone?" Henry asked.
"Maybe it fell into the bottom of your bag."
Maggie dumped her bag out on the bench.
"No, it's not here. Someone stole it! Just like all my other stuff!"
"Why would someone steal one sock?" Cole wondered.
Maggie didn't answer. She was already stomping down the aisle of the barn.
"Uh-oh," Henry said. "We'd better follow her."
He knew that his cousin had a quick temper.
If she started yelling about her sock, she might accidentally warn the thief that the boys were investigating.
Maggie stopped in front of a horse stall.
Daisy was standing in the doorway holding a saddle.
"My sock is missing!" Maggie said. "Did you take it?"
Daisy gave her a surprised look. "Why would I take your sock?
I have my own." She pointed to her feet.
Two pink socks were sticking out above her boots.
Henry grabbed Maggie's arm as Daisy went into her horse's stall.
"Wait," he said. "Yelling at people won't get your sock back."
"Or any of the other stuff," added Cole. "Let us investigate."
For a second Henry didn't think Maggie would agree. But finally she nodded.
"Okay," she said. "But how am I supposed to ride with only one sock?"
Cole kicked off his sneakers. "You can borrow one of mine," he said.
"Yuck. Boys' socks stink." Maggie made a face.
But she took the sock Cole handed her.
"I guess I'll have to suffer if I want to ride."
Then she stomped back toward Big Spot's stall.
Cole took off his other sock and stuck it in his pocket.
Then he put his shoes back on.
"Are we really going to investigate a missing sock?" he asked Henry.
"She probably just left it in the car or something."
"You could be right," Henry admitted.
"Did you notice if she had both socks in her bag when we came in?"
Cole laughed.
"No. I don't usually go around counting people's socks, especially when they're not even on their feet."
That gave Henry an idea. "I know what we can do," he said.
"Let's go see what socks everybody else is wearing.
For example, we know Daisy isn't wearing Maggie's missing sock.
Her socks are pink, and Maggie's are white."
"Do you really think someone took that sock?"
"Who knows?" Henry shrugged.
"Maybe someone forgot a sock and decided to borrow Maggie's since she wasn't watching it."

what?" Cole said. Henry looked at Nathan. "Why don't you
go see if anyone returned your painting?" he said. "Cole and
I will check in with Maggie." "Okay." Nathan didn't look very hopeful
as he hurried off.
Maggie was pouring lemonade for a middle-aged couple when Henry and Cole arrived. "Any news?" she asked as soon as
the couple left. Henry shook his head. "We
still haven't found Patrick or Mr. Collins. We did find Hannah, but
we only talked to her for a minute." He quickly described the encounter
with Hannah. "Have you seen any of our
suspects?" Cole asked Maggie. "Nope." Maggie patted the cashbox.
"I've sold a
lot of lemonade. But I haven't seen anything suspicious at all." "The woman
with the sunglasses didn't come back for her lemonade?" Henry asked. "Nope," Maggie
said again. Just then Nora hurried
over to the lemonade stand. "It's not right!" she announced loudly. "About
the painting of Patches, I mean." Henry was too distracted to
pay much attention to Nora. "We know," he told her. "We're
trying to find Nathan's painting. Don't worry." "No!"
Nora's voice was louder than ever. "It's
not right! Patches is my kitty. She shouldn't be in
a museum. She's mine—all mine! And the picture of her is mine too!"
Spinning around, Nora raced away.
"Nora?" Henry called. "Wait! What are you talking about?"
"Who cares?" Maggie said. "We care," Henry said. "What
if Nora took that painting?" Cole gasped. "That actually
makes sense! Well, as much
sense as anything Nora ever does, anyway. Nora seemed really upset when she heard Nathan's painting might end up
in the museum." "Exactly," Henry agreed. "And the stuff she was saying a minute ago
made her sound guilty."
"So are we adding her to the suspect list?" asked Maggie. "Definitely," Cole said. "She's
sneaky enough to snatch that painting
and hide it somewhere." "Luckily, we already know she's not very good
at covering her tracks," Henry said, smiling. He was
talking about an earlier case involving Nora, which
had led to her adopting Patches. "Let's go
look for clues at the scene of the crime." "Okay." Maggie put out the
Closed sign again. "How much time do we have before judging starts?" Henry glanced
at his phone. "Almost an hour." They
hurried over to the art show. When
they arrived at the empty spot where Nathan's painting had
been, Nathan wasn't there. But someone else was. "Hi, Mr.
Collins," Henry said. "What are you doing?" Mr.
Collins spun around and laughed sheepishly. "Oh! You
startled me." "Were you looking for Nathan's painting?" Maggie asked.
"Yes, I admit it." Mr. Collins tugged on his flowered tie. "It's been on my mind ever since I
saw it this morning. Can
you believe two artists found such similar inspiration? Young Nathan's subject could be the twin of mine!"
"Um, okay." Cole sounded doubtful. Henry knew what his friend was
thinking. Mr. Collins' crazy cat painting
looked nothing like Nathan's! "What if the judges think your paintings
are too similar?" Maggie asked. "Are you worried they might not
pick yours for the museum?" "I suppose not." Mr. Collins winked and smiled. "Nathan and I are not
even in the same age category, in case you couldn't
tell. I'm just worrying over nothing, as usual! It's the curse of
being a sensitive
artist." He glanced at the empty spot. "So
where is your friend's masterpiece?" "We're not sure," Henry said.
"It disappeared about forty minutes ago." "Oh dear!" Mr. Collins looked alarmed.
"Is there an art
thief at the show?" "Maybe," Cole said. "Have you seen anything suspicious?" "Where
have you been for the past hour?" Maggie demanded
before Mr. Collins could respond. Henry winced. Sometimes Maggie could sound rude when she
questioned people! Mr. Collins looked surprised. "Am I a suspect? Luckily I have
an alibi." "You do?" Henry was glad the man didn't seem
insulted. Mr. Collins nodded. "I've been at Mrs. Sweet's booth
for the past hour or so, learning how to make candy. She
could tell you that too." "Okay," Henry said. "Well,
we'd better get back to investigating." The
Lemonade Detectives hurried away. "Are we
going to check his alibi?" Maggie asked. Henry shrugged.
"I suppose we should, just to be sure. But I
bet he's telling the truth." "Yeah," Cole agreed. "His alibi explains why we couldn't find
him earlier." They walked toward the crafts fair.
As they passed the bandstand, Henry spotted Owen.
"Hi," Henry greeted him. "Have you seen Patrick?" Owen frowned.
"Not since I saw you guys earlier," he said. "We were
supposed to meet at the crafts fair ten minutes
ago. When he didn't show up, I came here to see if he was
at the burger stand. But he wasn't." Just then Henry
noticed a tall, thin
figure moving through the crowd. "Look," he
said. "It's that strange woman!" "Quick! We
have to catch her!" Cole took off, with
Henry and Maggie right behind him. The woman
was walking quickly toward the museum at the edge
of the park. "Excuse
me!" Henry yelled. "Wait up!" The woman glanced back.
When she saw Henry and the others coming, she gasped and
dashed toward the museum. She ran
up the steps, disappearing inside. "Stop!" Maggie yelled. The Lemonade Detectives ran
into the museum. It was cool
and dim inside. The sound of footsteps echoed off the walls, but Henry
couldn't tell which direction they were coming from. "This way!" Cole cried, pointing. Henry
turned just in time to see the woman
disappear around a corner. He ran after
her and burst into a large room filled with sculptures. "Where'd
she go?" Maggie
exclaimed. "There!" Henry cried. The Lemonade Detectives followed the woman through the
next room, which was filled with paintings. Then she escaped into
a hallway with lots of doors. Cole glanced
at all the doors. "Which way did she go?"
he asked breathlessly. A door leading outside was swinging shut.
Henry hurried over and
looked out into the Belltown Arts Day crowd. He sighed.
"I think we lost her."
